title: Modelling
text: This guide covers building a parametric model: parameters, sketch planes and profiles, the features that turn profiles into solids, SDF primitives, face references and constraints. The result is an SDF tree that functionalize turns into a pure JAX function of its parameters.

title: Modelling
text:
Example
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint import apply_parameters, extract_parameters, functionalize
from cadjoint.constraints import DistanceConstraint, FixedConstraint, solve_constraints
from cadjoint.construction import PolygonProfile, SketchPlane, extrude

profile = PolygonProfile(
    [[0.1, -0.1], [1.9, 0.2], [1.0, 1.5]],
    plane=SketchPlane(origin=[0.0, -0.5, 0.0], normal=[0.0, 0.0, 1.0]),
    name="tri",
)
v0, v1, v2 = profile.vertices
FixedConstraint(v0, [0.0, 0.0])
FixedConstraint(v1, [2.0, 0.0])
DistanceConstraint(v0, v2, 2.0)
DistanceConstraint(v1, v2, 2.0)

solved = solve_constraints(profile)     # {'tri_v0': ..., 'tri_v1': ..., 'tri_v2': [1, 1.732]}
apply_parameters(profile, solved)

solid = extrude(profile, depth=0.6)
free, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(solid)
sdf = functionalize(solid)(free, fixed)
sdf(jnp.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))         # negative: inside the triangle prism
Six vertex DOF and six constraint equations make the system exactly determined; the solution is an equilateral triangle with apex at (1, √3).

title: Modelling
text:
Parameters
Every number in a model is a parameter. A parameter carries a value, a free flag, an optional name and optional bounds.








Type
Value
Use




Scalar
float
Depths, radii, angles, offsets.


Vector2
2-vector
Sketch vertices, in the coordinates of a sketch plane.


Vector
3-vector
World positions and directions.



free=True marks a parameter as a design variable: it is differentiated, optimized and moved by the constraint solver. free=False (the default) makes it a fixed constant. Names key the parameter dicts that extract_parameters returns, so give every free parameter a unique name.
from cadjoint.geometry import Scalar, Vector, Vector2

p = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="p")
depth = Scalar(0.8, free=True, name="depth", bounds=(0.2, 2.0))
corner = Vector2([1.0, 0.0], free=True, name="corner")
Passing a plain number or array where a parameter is expected creates a fixed parameter. A PolygonProfile is the exception: its raw vertex arrays become free Vector2 parameters named <name>_v0, <name>_v1, ….

title: Modelling
text:
Sketch planes
A SketchPlane is a work plane: an origin, a normal and an in-plane x axis. Profile coordinates are 2D coordinates in that frame. SketchPlane() is the world XY plane at the origin.







Constructor
Plane




SketchPlane(origin, normal, x_axis=None)
Stated in world coordinates. x_axis pins the sketch’s horizontal; omit it for the derivation from the normal alone.


SketchPlane.on(face, x_axis=None, flip=False)
The face’s own plane, inheriting the face’s x axis: the profile’s u for a cap, the swept edge direction for a side wall.


SketchPlane.offset(face_or_plane, distance)
Pushed along the normal. distance may be a Scalar, so the clearance is a design variable.


SketchPlane.tangent(solid, near, x_axis=None)
Tangent to the field at the surface point nearest near. Horizontal defaults to the world axis most nearly in-plane.


SketchPlane.midplane(face_a, face_b)
Halfway between two faces.



The face-based constructors are described under Faces.

title: Modelling
text:
Profiles
A PolygonProfile is a closed polygon on a sketch plane. Its vertices are Vector2 parameters, two DOF each.
from cadjoint.construction import PolygonProfile, SketchPlane

tri = PolygonProfile(
    [[0.1, -0.1], [1.9, 0.2], [1.0, 1.5]],
    plane=SketchPlane(origin=[0.0, -0.5, 0.0], normal=[0.0, 0.0, 1.0]),
    name="tri",
)
tri.vertices    # [Vector2(..., free=True, name='tri_v0'), ..., name='tri_v2']
Vertices may also be existing Vector2 objects, so two profiles, or a profile and a constraint, can share them. free=False creates fixed vertices.
A profile belongs to the construction tree, not to the SDF. It is never rendered as geometry; render.draw_plane and render.draw_profile project the plane outline, the profile edges and the vertex handles through a render camera onto a matplotlib axis as a wireframe overlay.

title: Modelling
text:
Features
A feature generates an SDF solid from one or two profiles. The solid holds references to the profile’s vertex parameters, not copies, so the construction tree and the SDF tree share one parameter set: solving constraints on the sketch or differentiating through the solid acts on the same values.







Feature
Solid




extrude(profile, depth, material=None, draft=0.0, twist=0.0)
Prism spanning ±depth/2 around the sketch plane. draft (degrees) tapers the walls inward with increasing local z; the profile is exact at the bottom cap. twist (degrees over the full depth) rotates the section.


revolve(profile, offset=0.0, material=None)
Solid of revolution about the sketch plane’s local Y axis. Profile coordinates are (radial, height); offset is added to the radius. Keep the profile at positive radius.


loft(profile_a, profile_b, height, material=None)
Ruled solid between two profiles with equal vertex counts. Placed on profile_a’s plane, A at -height/2 and B at +height/2; vertex i of A connects to vertex i of B. Only profile_b’s 2D coordinates are used.



depth, height, offset, draft and twist accept a Scalar.
from cadjoint.construction import revolve

washer = PolygonProfile([[0.9, -0.18], [1.35, -0.28], [1.35, 0.28], [0.9, 0.18]], name="washer")
ring = revolve(washer)
ring.axis       # the world axis the profile was swept around

title: Modelling
text:
SDF primitives
Features produce SDF nodes; the same tree accepts standard primitives, booleans and transforms. Every node is differentiable in its parameters.







Group
Nodes




Primitives
Sphere, Box, RoundBox, Capsule, Cylinder, Torus, Plane


Booleans
Union, Intersection, Difference, Xor; operators a \| b (or a + b), a & b, a - b, a ^ b


Transforms
Translate, Rotate, Scale, Twist


Field transforms and patterns
Shell, Offset, Mirror, LinearPattern, PolarPattern


Measures
volume, material_mass



Booleans take a smoothness for a smooth blend (smooth_min / smooth_max). Each primitive takes an optional render material.
from cadjoint.sdf import Capsule, Rotate, Sphere, Translate, Twist, Union
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box

sphere = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.6), offset=jnp.array([-1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
box = Translate(Box(size=[0.7, 0.7, 1.0]), offset=jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.8]))
capsule = Translate(Capsule(radius=0.3, height=1.3), offset=jnp.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
scene = Union((sphere, box, capsule), smoothness=0.05)

turned = Rotate(scene, angle=jnp.pi / 2, axis=jnp.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]))
twisted = Twist(scene, strength=1.0, axis=jnp.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]))
Twist is a deformation: its field is not 1-Lipschitz, so it is not an exact distance. Solid.box, Solid.cylinder and Solid.sphere build primitives that carry faces (next section).

title: Modelling
text:
Faces
cadjoint stores no boundary representation. The dual-contoured mesh is extracted from the field at one resolution, so a work plane based on it would depend on the extraction grid.
The construction tree carries the faces instead. extrude spans ±depth/2 around its sketch plane, so it knows where its caps are and which plane each profile edge swept; a box knows its six faces; a revolve knows its axis. These are Face objects, and every generated solid carries them.
from cadjoint.construction import Solid

depth = Scalar(0.8, free=True, name="depth")
plate = PolygonProfile([[-1, -1], [1, -1], [1, 1], [-1, 1]], name="plate")
body = extrude(plate, depth=depth)

body.faces.keys()        # ['cap+', 'cap-', 'side0', 'side1', 'side2', 'side3']
body.cap("+").origin     # [0, 0, 0.4]: depth/2 along the sketch normal
body.side(0).normal      # [0, -1, 0]: the plane edge 0 swept

Solid.box(size=[1, 1, 1], position=[0, 0, 0], name="block").face("+z")
A Face holds its plane (origin, normal and an in-plane x axis, so a sketch’s horizontal is defined rather than derived from the normal), the polygon that bounds it, and a contains(point) test for world points.







Solid
Faces




extrude
cap+, cap-, side0 … sideN-1


loft
cap- (profile A), cap+ (profile B); ruled side walls are not declared


revolve
none; solid.axis is the reference


Solid.box
+x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z


drafted or twisted extrude
none; only SketchPlane.tangent applies




Work planes on faces
depth above is a free Scalar, so body.cap("+") is not a stored plane at z = 0.4 but the expression origin + (depth/2)·normal. A sketch on it follows the depth:
boss = PolygonProfile(
    [[-0.4, -0.4], [0.4, -0.4], [0.4, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.4]],
    plane=SketchPlane.on(body.cap("+")),
    name="boss",
)
The chain is differentiable:
def stack(depth):
    body = extrude(PolygonProfile([[-1, -1], [1, -1], [1, 1], [-1, 1]], name="p"), depth=depth)
    top = PolygonProfile([[-0.4, -0.4], [0.4, -0.4], [0.4, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.4]],
                         plane=SketchPlane.on(body.cap("+")), name="b")
    return extrude(top, depth=0.5)

probe = jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
jax.grad(lambda d: stack(d)(probe))(1.0)   # -0.5, exactly
The cap sits at half the depth, so the boss on it moves at half the rate, and the distance at a probe above the boss falls at exactly that rate.
In a B-rep CAD kernel a face is stored geometry that a rebuild replaces, and a downstream sketch is re-attached to it by a topological-naming heuristic, so reordering a feature can detach the sketch. Here the face is a function of the parent’s parameters: the reference cannot go stale, and it carries a derivative, so an optimizer moving depth moves everything referenced off it in the same step.


Tangent planes
Blends, fillets and revolved walls have no analytic face. A point projected onto the zero set gives a surface point, and the field gradient there is the normal:
dome = Sphere(radius=1.0)
pad = SketchPlane.tangent(dome, near=[0.0, 0.0, 0.9])   # plane at the north pole
The projection is a Newton iteration in JAX (cadjoint.fem.motion.project_points, the one-surface case of cadjoint.zeroset.project.project), so a tangent plane is differentiable with respect to the scene’s parameters; the pad moves out as the sphere grows.
Orientation is fixed when a solid is generated; origin is the differentiable part.

title: Modelling
text:
Functionalize
extract_parameters(tree) returns three things: the free parameters and the fixed parameters, each a dict keyed by name, and metadata that carries the constraint system. functionalize(tree)(free, fixed) returns the field as a pure JAX function of points, so jit, grad and vmap apply directly. apply_parameters(tree, values) is the inverse of extract_parameters: it writes a name-keyed dict back into the tree’s free parameters. A solid and its sketch share parameters, so applying to either updates both.
from cadjoint.sdf import Sphere, Translate

p = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="p")
scene = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.3), offset=p)
free, fixed, metadata = extract_parameters(scene)
field = functionalize(scene)(free, fixed)
field(jnp.zeros(3))     # 1.7

Compilation cache
functionalize(scene)(free, fixed) closes over the parameter values, so jax.jit of it folds every value into the program as a literal: two designs that differ in one value compile twice. functionalize_parametric takes the parameter dicts as arguments, so the lowered program is identical for every value and one executable serves them all. With the persistent compilation cache, a re-dimensioned design compiles nothing, even in a fresh process.
from cadjoint.cache import enable_compilation_cache
from cadjoint.functionalize import functionalize_parametric

enable_compilation_cache()      # ~/.cache/cadjoint/jax, or $CADJOINT_CACHE_DIR
evaluate = jax.jit(functionalize_parametric(scene))

evaluate(free, fixed, jnp.zeros(3))                                 # compiles once
evaluate({"p": jnp.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])}, fixed, jnp.zeros(3))    # reuses it
The playground’s compile worker enables the cache for every request; CADJOINT_NO_COMPILATION_CACHE=1 opts out. The stored programs are structured rather than flattened (a sketch profile is one (N, 2) array, a pattern traces its child once, a shared subtree is emitted once), which keeps them small enough to compile in under a second; see program size and the performance notes.

title: Modelling
text:
Constraints
A constraint is a relation between parameters. Constructing one registers it on its parameters; nothing is solved until a solver is called on a tree that contains them.

Constraint types








Constraint
Arguments
Equations




DistanceConstraint
param1, param2, distance
1


AngleConstraint
vector1, vector2, angle
1


ParallelConstraint
vector1, vector2
2


PerpendicularConstraint
vector1, vector2
1


FixedConstraint
param, target
one per component


CoincidentConstraint
point1, point2 (Vector2)
2


HorizontalConstraint
point1, point2 (Vector2)
1


VerticalConstraint
point1, point2 (Vector2)
1


PointOnLineConstraint
point, line1, line2 (Vector2)
1


EqualLengthConstraint
a1, a2, b1, b2 (Vector2 edges)
1


ParallelEdgesConstraint
a1, a2, b1, b2 (Vector2 edges)
1


PerpendicularEdgesConstraint
a1, a2, b1, b2 (Vector2 edges)
1



distance and angle accept a Scalar. Every constraint takes a keyword weight (default 1.0).


Degrees of freedom
A free parameter contributes one DOF per component: 1 for a Scalar, 2 for a Vector2, 3 for a Vector. Each constraint equation removes one. A system is exactly determined when the two counts match.
Trilateration: one free 3D point p (3 DOF) and three fixed anchors. One distance constraint leaves 2 DOF, and solve_constraints refuses it:
anchor_a = Vector(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="anchor_a")
anchor_b = Vector(jnp.array([4.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="anchor_b")
anchor_c = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 3.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="anchor_c")
true_p = jnp.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.0])

p = Vector(jnp.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.0]), free=True, name="p")     # wrong initial guess
scene = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.5), offset=p)

DistanceConstraint(p, anchor_a, float(jnp.linalg.norm(true_p - anchor_a.value)))
try:
    solve_constraints(scene)
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)    # Under-constrained: 2 DOF remaining. (3 parameter DOF, 1 constraint equations)
Each distance constraint is a sphere around its anchor; three of them meet at true_p. Adding the other two determines the system:
DistanceConstraint(p, anchor_b, float(jnp.linalg.norm(true_p - anchor_b.value)))
DistanceConstraint(p, anchor_c, float(jnp.linalg.norm(true_p - anchor_c.value)))

solved = solve_constraints(scene, max_steps=10)
solved["p"]     # [2.0, 1.0, 0.0], from the guess (0.5, 0.5, 0)

_, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(scene)
sdf = functionalize(scene)(solved, fixed)
sdf(true_p)     # -0.5: the solved sphere is centred on the true point


Solving









Function
Systems
Method
Writes back




solve_constraints(tree, tol=1e-6, max_steps=256)
Exactly determined only; raises ValueError otherwise
Levenberg–Marquardt (Optimistix)
No; returns the free-parameter dict, apply it with apply_parameters


satisfy_constraints(tree, steps=8, method="newton")
Any, including under-determined
"newton": minimum-norm projection onto the constraint manifold; "adam" / "sgd": Optax residual minimization
Yes, in place, and returns the dict



satisfy_constraints suits a sketch that keeps design freedom: unconstrained DOF stay near their current values.
from cadjoint.constraints import satisfy_constraints

q = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="q")
origin = Vector(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="origin")
DistanceConstraint(q, origin, 3.0)       # q must lie on a sphere of radius 3

satisfy_constraints(Translate(Sphere(radius=0.3), offset=q), steps=8)
float(jnp.linalg.norm(q.value))          # 3.0


Constraints during optimization
The metadata from extract_parameters carries the constraint system. project_to_manifold(params, metadata, steps) projects a parameter dict back onto it, so a descent can step and project. The optimizer does this automatically.
A quad with one anchored vertex and one pinned edge length (3 equations on 8 DOF), extruded and optimized toward a target volume:
from cadjoint.constraints import project_to_manifold
from cadjoint.sdf import volume

quad = PolygonProfile([[0.0, 0.0], [2.0, 0.0], [2.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]], name="quad")
q0, q1, q2, q3 = quad.vertices
FixedConstraint(q0, [0.0, 0.0])
DistanceConstraint(q0, q1, 2.0)

quad_solid = extrude(quad, depth=1.5)
free, fixed, meta = extract_parameters(quad_solid)
fn = functionalize(quad_solid)
target = 6.0

def loss(params):
    vol = volume(fn(params, fixed), bounds=(-1, -1, -1), size=(4, 4, 2), resolution=32)
    return (vol - target) ** 2

params = dict(free)
for _ in range(40):
    grads = jax.grad(loss)(params)
    params = {k: v - 0.05 * grads[k] for k, v in params.items()}
    params = project_to_manifold(params, meta, steps=2)

apply_parameters(quad, params)
float(jnp.linalg.norm(params["quad_v1"] - params["quad_v0"]))   # 2.0: still pinned
After 40 steps the volume, measured at resolution 64, is 6.28 against the target 6.0, and the pinned edge is still 2.0.

title: Modelling
text:
Limitations

Profiles are closed polygons. There are no arc or spline profile entities.
A drafted or twisted extrusion declares no analytic faces; a revolve declares none and exposes only its axis; a loft’s side walls are not declared.
Twist and a twisted extrude produce fields that are not 1-Lipschitz.
solve_constraints accepts only exactly determined systems.

title: Materials
text: A Material carries a part’s optical properties, which the renderer shades with, and its physical properties, which the solver reads in SI units. This page covers stating them, the catalogue of sourced values, free properties, the material field of a multi-material scene, and mass.

title: Materials
text:
Example
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.materials import aluminium_6061, copper_c11000
from cadjoint.sdf.boolean import Union
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box, Cylinder
from cadjoint.sdf.transforms import Translate

sink = Box([0.6, 0.6, 0.2], material=aluminium_6061())
slug = Translate(Cylinder(radius=0.2, height=0.4, material=copper_c11000()),
                 offset=jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.1]))
scene = Union((sink, slug), smoothness=0.03)

print(slug.material_at(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.1])).get("conductivity"))  # 391.0

title: Materials
text:
Properties
A Material has two families of properties:

Optical — color, roughness, metallic, opacity, ior, reflectivity. What the renderer shades with. Every one has a default, so a bare Material() is white matte plastic.
Physical — density, conductivity, specific_heat, youngs_modulus, poisson_ratio, thermal_expansion, yield_strength. What the solver solves with, in SI units. Every one defaults to None, meaning not specified.

Both families live in one object, so a scene states a material once: a slug declared as copper is orange, conducts 391 W/(m·K) and has a density of 8940 kg/m³.
from cadjoint.render import Material

copper = Material(
    name="copper",
    color=[0.72, 0.45, 0.20], roughness=0.30, metallic=1.0,
    density=8940.0, conductivity=391.0, specific_heat=385.0,
    youngs_modulus=117e9, poisson_ratio=0.34,
    thermal_expansion=17.0e-6, yield_strength=69e6,
)

title: Materials
text:
Unspecified properties
A physical property that is not stated has no default value.
Material(color=[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]).get("density")   # None
A study that needs a missing property fails and names it:
ValueError: study 'sink-conduction': the scene's material field does not
specify 'conductivity' for 6412 of 6412 elements. Give every material in the
simulated domain a 'conductivity' value (see cadjoint.materials for a
catalogue of real ones), or pass an explicit scalar to the study.
Internally an unstated property is NaN in as_dict(), so the material dict keeps one static pytree structure across a scene, and blending an unstated value with a stated one yields NaN.

cadjoint.materials ships sourced values. Each entry is a factory, not a singleton, so marking one scene’s copper free does not affect another scene. The example builds a scene from two of them.

Every factory’s docstring cites its sources — MatWeb and ASM datasheets for the metals, the CRC Handbook for the elements, NEMA/IPC and laminate datasheets for FR-4, Hopcroft et al. (JMEMS 2010) for silicon’s modulus, NatureWorks and Farah et al. for PLA.
Three entries have caveats, also stated in their docstrings:

FR-4 is orthotropic. The entry takes the through-thickness conductivity (0.29, versus ~0.8–1.0 in plane) and the in-plane elastic constants, the values that usually govern the result. yield_strength holds the ultimate tensile strength — FR-4 is brittle and has no yield plateau.
Silicon is elastically anisotropic; the entry uses ⟨100⟩ (E = 130 GPa). Its yield_strength is a conservative practical fracture strength, which in reality is dominated by edge and surface damage.
The thermal pad has ν = 0.49. Elastomers are nearly incompressible, and linear HEX8/TET4 elements lock volumetrically there. Use TET10, or lower the ratio, if the pad’s compliance matters.

title: Materials
text:
Free properties
Physical properties use the same Parameter containers as colors, so an optimizer can tune them:
tunable = Material("tim", conductivity=3.0, free=True)
tunable.params["conductivity"].free     # True
tunable.params["conductivity"].bounds   # (0.001, 3000.0)
free=True marks only the properties the material states. The bounds are wide engineering brackets (aerogel to tungsten) that keep a descent physical; they do not encode a material choice.

title: Materials
text:
Material fields
Every SDF node answers material_at(p), and the smooth booleans blend the answers. A scene built from several materials is therefore a continuous field of physical properties: copper’s conductivity inside the slug, aluminium’s outside, and a transition as wide as the CSG blend between them.
The simulation layer samples this field per element at solve time; see material properties. Moving the interface moves the property field smoothly, so the gradient flows through it.

title: Materials
text:
Mass
With densities on the materials, mass is computable and differentiable, so it can regularize an optimization:
from cadjoint.sdf import material_mass, volume

lattice = dict(bounds=(-0.7, -0.7, -0.3), size=(1.4, 1.4, 0.8), resolution=70)
print(float(volume(scene, **lattice)))          # 0.609  m³, shape only
print(float(material_mass(scene, **lattice)))   # 2074.6 kg, weighted by what each region is
material_mass takes the same arguments as volume: a sampling box, a resolution, and the epsilon of the sigmoid that softens the boundary. It also accepts an explicit sample lattice, the form a scene’s regularizer usually has:
import jax
from cadjoint import extract_parameters, functionalize

free, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(scene)
sdf = functionalize(scene)(free, fixed)
axis = jnp.linspace(-0.7, 0.7, 70)
cells = jnp.stack(jnp.meshgrid(axis, axis, axis, indexing="ij"), -1).reshape(-1, 3)
cell_volume = float(axis[1] - axis[0]) ** 3

# a volume regularizer …
cell_volume * jnp.sum(jax.nn.sigmoid(-jax.vmap(sdf)(cells) / 0.03))
# … and the same thing weighted by what each cell is made of
material_mass(scene, cells, cell_volume, epsilon=0.03)
For a single-material part the two differ by a constant factor; for a design that trades copper for aluminium only mass is meaningful. On a mesh, cadjoint.fem.properties.total_mass(points, cells, density) gives the exact element-wise sum instead of a lattice estimate, and a solved study reports it as result.mass.

title: Materials
text:
Inspection
describe() returns the JSON payload the playground’s Materials window reads and edits, physical properties included, as source rewrites:
Material("al", color=[0.8, 0.8, 0.82], density=2700.0, conductivity=167.0).describe()
{
  "color": [0.8, 0.8, 0.82],
  "roughness": 0.5, "metallic": 0.0, "opacity": 1.0,
  "ior": 1.0, "reflectivity": 0.0,
  "physical": {
    "density": 2700.0, "conductivity": 167.0,
    "specific_heat": null, "youngs_modulus": null,
    "poisson_ratio": null, "thermal_expansion": null,
    "yield_strength": null
  },
  "units": {"density": "kg/m^3", "conductivity": "W/(m*K)", "…": "…"},
  "free": {"color": false, "density": false, "…": false}
}
physical values are floats or null; units names the SI unit of each so a panel can label a field without hard-coding it; free flags which properties an optimizer controls.

title: Getting started
text: cadjoint is code-first CAD in which sketches, constraints, SDF geometry, meshing and finite-element simulation compose into one function JAX can differentiate end to end. This page installs it, builds one model, takes one gradient, and links to the guide for each stage.

title: Getting started
text:
Install
From PyPI, pinned because the API moves:
pip install "cadjoint==<version>"
From a checkout, with uv:
git clone https://github.com/andrinr/cadjoint
cd cadjoint
uv sync                      # CPU JAX: macOS, Linux, Windows
uv sync --extra cuda         # Linux + NVIDIA GPU instead
uv sync creates .venv and installs cadjoint into it in editable mode. Run commands through it with uv run <cmd>, or activate it with source .venv/bin/activate. Everything beyond the geometry core is an extra, one --extra per name (uv sync --extra fem --extra tesseract --extra viewer); the extras table lists what each pulls in.
fem is the one extra that compiles. petsc4py publishes no wheels, so uv sync --extra fem builds PETSc from source and needs a C compiler, gfortran and BLAS/LAPACK headers (apt install build-essential gfortran libopenblas-dev on Debian/Ubuntu). Without that toolchain, run the solvers as Tesseracts instead: their images get PETSc from conda-forge and are published prebuilt to GHCR for amd64 and arm64, so Docker is the only requirement (see prebuilt images).

Supported platforms








Platform
uv sync
uv sync --extra fem




Linux x86_64
yes
compiles PETSc


Linux ARM64
yes
no: gmsh has no Linux ARM wheel


macOS arm64
yes
compiles PETSc


macOS x86_64 (Intel)
no: jaxlib has no Intel-Mac wheel for Python 3.11+
no


Windows x86_64
yes
no: PETSc does not build natively



Every “yes” is a fresh uv sync --locked and import cadjoint in install.yml, run on each push. Where the fem column says no, the prebuilt solver Tesseracts run the same solvers in Docker.

title: Getting started
text:
A first model
A four-vertex sketch with one distance constraint, extruded by a free depth and dual-contoured into a mesh:
from cadjoint.construction import PolygonProfile, SketchPlane, extrude
from cadjoint.constraints import DistanceConstraint, satisfy_constraints
from cadjoint.geometry import Scalar, Vector2
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec, extract_mesh, save_stl

a = Vector2([0.0, 0.0], free=True, name="a")
b = Vector2([1.0, 0.0], free=True, name="b")
c = Vector2([1.0, 1.0], free=True, name="c")
d = Vector2([0.0, 1.0], free=True, name="d")
DistanceConstraint(a, b, 1.2)

depth = Scalar(0.5, free=True, name="depth")
block = extrude(PolygonProfile([a, b, c, d], plane=SketchPlane()), depth=depth)
satisfy_constraints(block)          # projects a and b onto the constraint, in place

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (2.0, 2.0, 1.5), 32)
mesh = extract_mesh(block, grid)
save_stl(mesh, "block.stl")
Parameters, sketches, features and constraints are covered in Modelling; the mesher and its exporters in Meshing.

title: Getting started
text:
Gradients
extract_parameters splits the tree into free and fixed parameter dicts, and functionalize turns it into a pure function of them. jax.grad of anything downstream reaches every free parameter:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint import extract_parameters, functionalize

free, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(block)
field = functionalize(block)
probe = jnp.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5])

grads = jax.grad(lambda params: field(params, fixed)(probe))(free)
grads["depth"]      # -0.5: the top cap sits at depth/2
The probe lies above the top cap, so only depth moves its distance; the vertex gradients there are zero.
Optimization runs this gradient through a mesh and a finite-element solve.

title: Getting started
text:
Playground
The browser app ships in the package and needs the viewer extra (editor adds lint and completion):
uvx --from "cadjoint[viewer,editor]" cadjoint-viewer --open   # nothing installed
uv run --extra viewer --extra editor cadjoint-viewer --open   # from a checkout
It opens on a parametric heat sink that declares a mesh, a thermal study and an optimization. See the playground.

title: Getting started
text:
Scripts
Run from the repository root with python examples/<name>.py.

fem_bracket_optimization.py: shape optimization of an L-bracket through SDF, hex mesh and linear elastic solve (jax-fem or CalculiX), minimizing compliance and mass with Adam; writes a convergence CSV, a plot and VTK files to examples/output/. Requires the fem extra and optax.
rendering_gallery.py: renders the lighting-mode and quality-preset comparison images in Rendering to docs/assets/.

title: Getting started
text:
Next

Modelling: parameters, sketches, features, SDF solids, faces and constraints.
Meshing: dual contouring, sharp features, export and mesh checks.
Simulation: simulation meshes, thermal and elastic studies, solver backends.
Materials: the Material class, the catalogue, material fields and mass.
Optimization: declared descents, objectives, gradient paths and constraints.
Rendering: the JAX raymarcher, quality presets and WGSL compilation.
Plugins: the plugin contract, plugins.toml, and writing and serving a plugin.
Flow solver (prototype): lattice-Boltzmann flow and conjugate heat transfer on the SDF.

title: cadjoint
text:
cadjoint is differentiable code-first CAD. Sketches, constraints, SDF geometry, meshing and finite-element simulation compose into one function JAX can differentiate end to end.
The playground runs the whole chain in the browser (modelling, meshing, studies and optimization) and writes every edit back into the Python source.
pip install cadjoint installs the library. Getting started covers installation, supported platforms and the playground command; the playground guide covers the app.

title: cadjoint
text:
Components



Layer
What it does




Geometry
Parametric Vector / Scalar carrying free / fixed flags


SDF
Primitives, booleans and transforms, all differentiable


Sketches
2D profiles on work planes, extruded or revolved into solids that share their parameters


Constraints
Geometric relationships that reduce DOF, with Newton projection onto the constraint manifold


Functionalize
Convert a parametric scene to a pure JAX function for jit / grad / vmap


Meshing
Dual contouring built bottom-up in JAX; exact gradients through every continuous stage; OBJ / STL / STEP export


Simulation
Declared SimMesh and thermal/elastic studies, node selections, and pluggable solver backends


Flow
A prototype lattice-Boltzmann conjugate heat-transfer solver on the scene’s own field, with no mesh


Optimization
Declarative descent over named CAD parameters with the simulation as objective


Plugins
Meshers and solvers behind one apply/vjp contract, so one jax.grad crosses every tool boundary


Rendering
Forward sphere tracing, plus StableHLO → WGSL shader compilation


The playground
The whole toolchain as a browser app, with the Python source as its only state

title: cadjoint
text:
Pipeline
CAD parameters θ  ──►  constraints ──► SDF        (JAX autodiff)
        │                              │
        │                              ▼
        │                  dual-contoured surface   (JAX autodiff:
        │                              │             Newton on the true SDF)
        │                              ▼
        │              ┌─ tetfill Tesseract ─────┐ (TetGen; frozen topology,
        │              │  surface → TET4/TET10   │  exact pass-through VJP)
        │              └───────────┬─────────────┘
        │                          ▼
        │              ┌─ solver Tesseract ──────┐ (jax-fem adjoint, or
        │              │  thermal / elastic FEM  │  CalculiX Fortran adjoint)
        │              └───────────┬─────────────┘
        │                          ▼
        └──────────  ∂J/∂θ  ◄──  objective J      (JAX autodiff)
No two stages compute their derivative the same way, and TetGen has none; the frozen-topology pass-through supplies it. On the parametric L-bracket the composed loop lowers the objective 73% in 30 steps, with the adjoint checked against finite differences at every boundary.

title: cadjoint
text:
Quick start
Three distance constraints determine an unknown point; the solved scene is an ordinary JAX function.
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint import extract_parameters, functionalize
from cadjoint.constraints import DistanceConstraint, solve_constraints
from cadjoint.geometry.parameters import Vector
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Sphere
from cadjoint.sdf.transforms import Translate

# Unknown point — wrong initial guess
p = Vector(jnp.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.0]), free=True, name="p")
scene = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.5), offset=p)

# Fixed anchors
anchor_a = Vector(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="a")
anchor_b = Vector(jnp.array([4.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="b")
anchor_c = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 3.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="c")
true_p = jnp.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.0])

for anchor in (anchor_a, anchor_b, anchor_c):
    DistanceConstraint(p, anchor, float(jnp.linalg.norm(true_p - anchor.value)))

solved = solve_constraints(scene)
_, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(scene)
sdf = functionalize(scene)(solved, fixed)

print(sdf(true_p))  # ≈ -0.5 — the solved sphere is centred on the true point
Modelling covers constraints and degrees of freedom; the guides continue through meshing, simulation and optimization.

title: Flow solver
text: cadjoint.flow solves forced convection over a part (air pushed along a duct, heat conducted out of the part and carried away by the air) on a fixed lattice, and differentiates the pressure drop and the temperature with respect to the geometry with no mesh generation in the loop.

title: Flow solver
text:
Example
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

from cadjoint import extract_parameters, functionalize
from cadjoint.flow import FlowConfig, FlowGrid, SteadyOptions, sample_solid_fraction, solve
from cadjoint.geometry import Vector
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box

fin = Box(Vector([0.3, 0.4, 0.6], free=True, name="size"))
free, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(fin)
evaluate = functionalize(fin)

grid = FlowGrid(shape=(16, 32, 16), origin=(-1.0, -2.0, -1.0), size=(2.0, 4.0, 2.0))
chi = sample_solid_fraction(evaluate(free, fixed), grid)
print(chi.shape, float(chi.max()), grid.suggested_epsilon())   # (16, 32, 16) 1.0 0.0625

config = FlowConfig(
    shape=grid.shape, inlet_speed=0.02, reynolds=30.0,
    steady=SteadyOptions(tol=1e-10, adjoint_solver="fixed_point",
                         adjoint_tol=1e-10, adjoint_max_steps=4000),
)
print(round(config.omega, 4), round(config.mach, 3))   # 1.8797 0.035

result = solve(chi, config, cell_volume=grid.cell_volume)
print(float(result.pressure_drop), float(result.heat_transfer))

title: Flow solver
text:
Brinkman penalisation
The scene’s SDF is sampled on a fixed lattice and mapped to a solid fraction chi(x) in [0, 1]. chi enters the momentum equation as a Brinkman drag −alpha_max · chi · u, which stops the fluid where the design is solid. The grid never moves, so the chain from a sketch point to a pressure drop is one JAX expression:
sketch point → SDF → chi = profile(−f(x) / ε) → alpha = alpha_max · chi
             → D3Q19 lattice-Boltzmann fixed point → pressure drop, heat proxy

title: Flow solver
text:
Grid and solid fraction
FlowGrid is the lattice in world coordinates, with the duct along +Y; sample_solid_fraction evaluates a scene SDF on it. The profile that maps distance to occupancy has compact support, because a sigmoid never reaches zero and, multiplied by alpha_max, its tail blocks every open channel. The default is a C² quintic, which also keeps a finite-difference check second order.

title: Flow solver
text:
Solver settings
FlowConfig holds the lattice-unit settings (inlet speed, Reynolds number, drag at chi = 1) and derives the BGK relaxation rate omega from them. It rejects an omega above 1.95 at construction: BGK loses stability as omega approaches 2, and the penalised solid lowers that limit.
FlowResult carries the converged populations, density and velocity fields and two scalars: the inlet-to-outlet pressure_drop, and heat_transfer, an ∫ chi |u| proxy for a cooling number without an energy solve. FlowStudy (below) reports a temperature and is the recommended objective. convergence returns the residual history.

title: Flow solver
text:
Gradients
Nothing in the chain contours, meshes or decides membership, so jax.grad runs through the SDF, the profile and the fixed point:
def objective(free):
    chi = sample_solid_fraction(evaluate(free, fixed), grid)
    return solve(chi, config, cell_volume=grid.cell_volume).pressure_drop

value, grad = jax.value_and_grad(objective)(free)
print(float(value), grad["size"])
# 0.0039086 [6.884e-04 2.700e-03 8.27e-07]
Widening the fin across the duct (size[0]) raises the pressure drop at 6.9e-4 per unit; lengthening it along the flow (size[1]) costs about four times as much, and its height (size[2]) almost nothing, because the box already spans most of the duct’s height. A central difference on size[0] with h = 1e-3 gives 6.897e-4, 0.2 % from the adjoint, which is the difference scheme’s truncation. On the starter sink’s sketch handles the research note measures 3e-8.
The gradient comes from the implicit function theorem rather than from taping the pseudo-time march: one adjoint solve at the converged state, with memory independent of the number of steps. On the starter sink that is 457 MB against the tape’s 21 GB, and the two agree to 5.6e-11 once the tape’s march has converged.







adjoint_solver
Behaviour




"gmres"
fastest when it converges; holds restart Krylov vectors


"fixed_point"
Richardson iteration on the same system; converges exactly when the forward march does; three states of memory



Disagreement between the two means one solve had not converged. The default adjoint_max_steps of 400 is too few on this duct for either solver (with it, the example reports 8.1e-4 rather than 6.9e-4), so the configuration above raises it. Check a new configuration against a finite difference once.

title: Flow solver
text:
Conjugate heat transfer
A FlowStudy declares the coupled problem the way a ThermalStudy declares conduction (in the scene, captured by capture_studies, with describe() and its own boundary conditions) and solves both the flow and the temperature. On the fin box from above:
from cadjoint.studies import Nodes
from cadjoint.flow import FlowStudy, HeatSource, Inlet, Outlet, Walls

cooling = FlowStudy(
    name="duct-cooling",
    resolution=(20, 26, 12),        # cubic cells: 1.40/20 = 1.82/26 = 0.84/12
    bounds=(-0.70, -0.91, -0.50), size=(1.40, 1.82, 0.84),
    reynolds=25.0, conductivity_ratio=200.0,
    bcs=[
        Inlet(velocity=0.02, temperature=0.0),
        Outlet(),
        Walls(),                       # no-slip always; adiabatic by default
        HeatSource(Nodes.box([-0.14, -0.18, -0.42], [0.14, 0.18, -0.18]), power=1.0),
    ],
)
result = cooling.solve(evaluate(free, fixed))
print(float(result.peak_temperature), float(result.pressure_drop))
scenes/duct_sink.py declares the same study around a three-fin sink. python scenes/duct_sink.py runs in well under a minute and prints:
peak temperature     0.42973      thermal resistance   0.42973
mean temperature     0.41265      pressure drop        0.010414
outlet bulk air      0.27618      energy imbalance    -2.566e-11
The cells must be cubic. The solve is entirely in lattice units (streaming moves one cell per axis, the energy stencil is one cell wide), so size only decides where the SDF is sampled, and a lattice with unequal spacings solves the duct stretched by their ratio.
A scene declaring a flow study opens, renders and compiles in the playground, and the Studies window reads and edits it like any other study.

Energy equation
The energy equation is solved once over the whole lattice, with the conductivity interpolated by chi between the air’s and the solid’s:
div(k grad T)  =  (rho cp)_f  u · grad T  −  q
Inside the metal u is zero (removed by the Brinkman drag), so the equation reduces to conduction; in the channels k is the air’s and advection dominates. No interface condition is imposed: one unknown field admits no temperature jump, and a conservative finite-volume flux is shared by the cells on either side of a face, so temperature and heat flux are continuous by construction, with no interface to locate or mesh.
The coupling is one-way, which is exact in this model: the momentum solve takes chi, an inlet velocity and a viscosity, none of which depends on temperature. Two-way coupling would add buoyancy, which is negligible at small Richardson number; result.richardson reports it (2.1e-4 on scenes/duct_sink.py).


Volumetric selections
HeatSource and HeldTemperature take the same Nodes.box / sphere / halfspace / cylinder selections as a mesh study, composed with &, | and ~. A lattice has no boundary surface, so a selection picks every cell centre satisfying the criterion rather than boundary nodes. Nodes.side and Nodes.predicate are rejected with the alternative named. A region thinner than a cell contains no centres and is rejected as well.


Warnings
result.warnings() reports:

a lattice whose cells are not cubes, which solves a stretched duct;
a Richardson number above 0.1;
a Reynolds number past the turbulent transition;
an under-resolved thermal boundary layer;
an energy balance that does not close.



Gradient through both solves
d(peak temperature)/d(geometry) runs through the momentum fixed point’s adjoint and the energy solve’s transposed linear solve, which are independent:
from cadjoint.flow.precision import double_precision

def objective(parameters):
    return cooling.solve(evaluate(parameters, fixed)).peak_temperature

with double_precision():
    gradient = jax.grad(objective)(free)
Against a central difference on a box in a duct, the difference converges to the adjoint at second order, down to 4.6e-8 relative. On a new configuration, check the convergence rate, not one step size: where a perturbation puts the surface exactly on a plane of cell centres, the objective has a kink and the difference converges only at first order. It still converges to the adjoint, but a single ratio at a single h cannot distinguish that from a wrong gradient.


Precision
The solve needs float64 and enables it for the duration of the call. A scene therefore sets no jax flags: setting jax_enable_x64 at module scope would make the whole process float64, and the WGSL backend has no 64-bit type, so the scene would not open in the viewer.
The scope covers a forward solve but not a gradient, because jax.grad runs its backward pass after the call returns. Differentiating through a study needs x64 around the gradient, as with the FEM solvers: double_precision() above, or precision="double" on an Optimization. Without it the backward pass fails with lax.dynamic_update_slice requires arguments to have the same dtypes, got float32, float64.


Verification







Check
Result




pure conduction vs. the analytic parabola
3.9e-3 → 6.1e-5 over 8 → 64 cells, exactly 2nd order


the same problem on the FEM ThermalStudy
agrees to 2.4e-4 of the peak at 32 cells (all of it the lattice’s truncation; the FEM side is exact to 1e-14)


metal–air interface vs. a two-layer series resistance
1.4e-13 at a conductivity ratio of 8000


advection–diffusion vs. the analytic column
3.9e-16 (exponential scheme); upwind is off by 0.198


square-duct Nusselt number vs. the textbook 2.976
2.927 at 22 cells across (−1.65%), 2.857 at 14 (−4.0%)


global energy balance
2.6e-11 of the injected power

title: Flow solver
text:
Shape optimization
scenes/duct_fairing.py optimizes one blunt body immersed in a duct, with the pressure drop of the converged flow as the objective. Run from the repository root:
from cadjoint.optimize import Optimization
from scenes.duct_fairing import fairing, streamlining_cost

streamline = Optimization(
    name="streamline",
    objective=streamlining_cost,   # dp / dp_ref + 6 (V/V_ref - 1)^2
    of=fairing,                    # the box's free half-extents
    steps=16, learning_rate=0.005, method="adam",
    precision="double",
)
The volume term is required because pressure drop alone is minimized by removing the obstacle. In a duct the pressure drop is dominated by blockage, so at constant volume the descent trades frontal area for length. At the starting box d(dp)/d(half-width) = +5.709e-2 across the flow against +1.242e-2 along it.
Sixteen steps take about two and a half minutes on a laptop CPU:
aspect (y/x)  0.750 -> 1.011      frontal area  0.16000 -> 0.13277
volume        0.04800 -> 0.04892  pressure drop 4.597e-3 -> 2.684e-3
The volume drifts 1.9%, so the scene also solves the start box scaled isotropically to the final volume. It costs 4.706e-3 against 2.684e-3 for the optimized shape at the same volume: a 43% reduction from proportions alone.
main() verifies the gradient on every run: it asserts that the relative error against a central difference falls by about 100× when the step size falls by 10×, the second-order convergence that the "smootherstep" solid-fraction profile preserves.
A heat-sink objective needs both temperature and pressure drop: on scenes/duct_sink.py the sink costs 11.7× the empty duct’s pressure drop while holding the die 0.430 above inlet air, and thickening a fin moves the two in opposite directions. Without the pressure term an optimizer converges to a solid block. One FlowStudy reports both.

title: Flow solver
text:
Plugin
The solver ships as flow_brinkman, a plugin of kind flow_solver. The other solver plugins take a mesh; this one takes one array:
from cadjoint.plugins import plugin_for_kind

flow = plugin_for_kind("flow_solver")
print(flow.name, sorted(flow.capabilities.differentiable_inputs))
# flow_brinkman ['chi', 'inlet_velocity']
apply and vector_jacobian_product through the runtime are bit-identical to the in-process solve and gradient, because both sides run the same custom_vjp. It needs no conda and no extra: cadjoint.flow is pure JAX.

title: Flow solver
text:
Limitations

The model is laminar. A forced-convection heat sink often runs above the duct transition at Re ≈ 2300, where this solver reports the laminar answer and so overstates the temperature.
It runs on CPU at 12–16 million lattice updates a second, about 2 % of the memory roofline, because stream() is nineteen jnp.rolls where a fused kernel makes one pass. Iterations to convergence grow linearly with the grid’s linear size (about 119·N + 1400), so a 128³ solve takes 48 minutes on this CPU and four minutes on an A100 as written.
A Nusselt number within a couple of percent needs about 22 cells across a channel; the examples here use 12 to 16.
Adjoint memory: GMRES at 128³ holds 12.8 GB of Krylov vectors.
The design space is a few primitive dimensions.
Read §8.9 of the research note before quoting an absolute number; it lists which results speed, turbulence and a wider design space would change.

title: Meshing
text: cadjoint.meshing turns a signed distance field into a surface mesh by dual contouring, with an exact derivative through every continuous stage, and SimMesh turns that surface into a tet or hex volume mesh for the solvers.

title: Meshing
text:
Example
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec, extract_mesh

def sphere_sdf(p):
    return jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(p * p)) - 1.0

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -1.3, -1.3), (2.6, 2.6, 2.6), 26)
mesh = extract_mesh(sphere_sdf, grid)

print(mesh.vertices.shape, mesh.faces.shape, mesh.quads.shape)
# (1832, 3) (3660, 3) (1830, 4)

title: Meshing
text:
Extraction
GridSpec describes the sampling lattice; extract_mesh runs the whole chain and returns a Mesh. GridSpec.from_bounds(bounds, size, resolution) takes a corner, an extent, and either one cell count or a per-axis triple. A Mesh is a NamedTuple of vertices and normals (JAX arrays, one per active cell), faces (triangles), quads (the native dual-contour output), and cells (the lattice index each vertex came from).
extract_mesh defaults to sharp=True, which places vertices with a rank-revealing SVD so creases and corners stay sharp. That path is forward-only, because the SVD truncation is not differentiable. Pass sharp=False for the Tikhonov-regularized QEF, which is smooth and differentiable everywhere.

title: Meshing
text:
Gradients
Which lattice edges cross the surface, which cells are active and how cells connect are discrete choices, frozen per extraction and not differentiable. Crossing positions, Hermite normals and QEF vertices are continuous and carry derivatives. An optimization loop holds topology fixed while gradients flow through node positions, and re-extracts every few steps.
To differentiate, sample the lattice, freeze the discrete structure, then rebuild only the continuous stages inside the traced function.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.meshing import (
    GridSpec, edge_hermite_data, find_crossing_edges,
    manifold_cell_incidence, qef_vertices, sample_grid,
)

def sphere(radius):
    return lambda p: jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(p * p)) - radius

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -1.3, -1.3), (2.6, 2.6, 2.6), 26)

# Discrete half — frozen once, outside the gradient.
values = sample_grid(sphere(1.0), grid)
edges = find_crossing_edges(values)
incidence = manifold_cell_incidence(edges, grid, values < 0.0)

# Continuous half — re-evaluated under the trace.
def loss(radius):
    hermite = edge_hermite_data(sphere(radius), grid, edges)
    vertices, _ = qef_vertices(hermite, incidence, grid)
    return jnp.sum(vertices ** 2)

print(jax.grad(loss)(jnp.float32(1.0)))  # 3638.59
The gradient is exact. Root finding runs bisection and secant iterations on stop_gradient values, then applies one differentiable Newton correction, t = t0 - f(x(t0)) / (df/dt). At a converged root its derivative is the implicit-function-theorem value dt/dθ = -(∂f/∂θ) / (∂f/∂t), independent of how the root was found.
Bisection is also a correctness choice. Hard CSG enters the field through jnp.minimum / jnp.maximum, which makes it piecewise smooth; a bracketing method keyed on sign is unaffected by the kink, and the one-sided Hermite normals at a seam are the subgradients dual contouring needs to reconstruct a crease.

title: Meshing
text:
Stages
extract_mesh composes stages that are individually public, so a caller can substitute or instrument any of them. The stage-to-test map and the benchmark policy are in the meshing pipeline note.

Diagnostics

Features are classified two ways. classify_feature_cells measures normal spread with an SVD and reports each cell as FACE, CREASE, or CORNER. active_branches and detect_branch_changes are exact instead of thresholded: they record which CSG branch wins the min/max at each sample, and a cell where the winner changes is a seam, with no tolerance to tune.

Adaptive octree
Sampling the full lattice is wasteful when the surface occupies a thin shell of it. surface_cells and sparse_crossing_edges prune with an octree that descends only into blocks whose distance bound admits a crossing. The results are bit-identical to dense detection; lipschitz is the caller’s contract that the field does not grow faster than that bound (1.0 for a true distance function).
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec, surface_cells
import jax.numpy as jnp

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -1.3, -1.3), (2.6, 2.6, 2.6), 26)
stats = {}
cells = surface_cells(lambda p: jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(p * p)) - 1.0,
                      grid, lipschitz=1.0, stats=stats)
print(cells.shape[0], stats["evaluations"])  # 2216 5857
That is 5857 field evaluations instead of the 19683 lattice points of a dense sweep, for the same set of crossings.

title: Meshing
text:
Diagnostics
mesh_report bundles four diagnostics: watertightness, Euler characteristic, surface deviation and triangle quality.
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec, extract_mesh, mesh_report

sdf = lambda p: jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(p * p)) - 1.0
grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -1.3, -1.3), (2.6, 2.6, 2.6), 26)
mesh = extract_mesh(sdf, grid)

report = mesh_report(sdf, mesh, samples=512, pairs=1024, seed=1)
print(report["watertight"], report["euler_characteristic"])
print(report["surface_deviation"])
# True 2
# {'max_abs': 0.00294, 'mean_abs': 0.00083, 'samples': 512}
Surface deviation evaluates the true field at points sampled on the mesh, measuring how far the discretization strays from the geometry: a maximum absolute error of 0.0029 on a unit sphere at 26 cells.

title: Meshing
text:
Export
Three writers, each taking a Mesh and a path:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec, extract_mesh, save_obj, save_step, save_stl

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -1.3, -1.3), (2.6, 2.6, 2.6), 26)
mesh = extract_mesh(lambda p: jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(p * p)) - 1.0, grid)

save_obj(mesh, "part.obj")    # merge_planar=True by default
save_stl(mesh, "part.stl")    # binary=True by default
save_step(mesh, "part.step")  # AP214 faceted BREP, metres
save_obj merges coplanar triangles into n-gons first, so a flat wall exports as one face rather than a fan of triangles; merge_planar_faces exposes that directly with an angle and plane tolerance. save_step writes a CLOSED_SHELL inside a MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP and is validated against the OCCT kernel in tests/meshing/test_step_kernel.py.
All three write the mesh as it is, so the export is a faceted solid: one triangle per cell crossing, a 28-gon standing in for a bore. The STEP has real B-rep topology (an ADVANCED_FACE per merged polygon over its own PLANE, so a CAD kernel opens it as one closed solid rather than a triangle soup), but its faces are the mesh’s faces, and a bore arrives as the ring of narrow facets the lattice cut it into. A STEP in which a plate with a hole is seven faces instead of three thousand, the bore one CYLINDRICAL_SURFACE, is the job of the step_export plugin kind; with nothing registered for it, exports use the writers on this page and the report says so.

title: Meshing
text:
Program size
Every stage above evaluates the scene’s SDF under jax.jit, so the wall clock of a first mesh is mostly XLA compiling one program per stage, and the size of those programs is decided by functionalize, not by the mesher. Three measures keep the tree from flattening as it is traced:

A sketch profile’s vertices are stacked into one (N, 2) array and its edge loop becomes two reductions, so a 168-vertex profile emits the same operations as a 12-vertex one.
A pattern traces its child once, over an array of instance transforms, and a node reachable from more than one parent is built once and outlined into its own StableHLO function.
Passing the parameter dicts to the jitted function rather than closing over them (functionalize_parametric) keeps values out of the program entirely, so a re-dimensioned design reuses the executable the compilation cache already holds.

On scenes/end_cap.py (eight gusset ribs, three polar bolt circles, a mirrored dowel) these reduce the gradient program from 1.62 MB / 18 090 operations to 0.58 MB / 5 771, and its XLA compile from 25.4 s to 0.68 s.

title: Meshing
text:
Volume meshes
SimMesh builds the volume mesh a solver uses; see simulation. The same declared resolution means different things per method. method="hex" only decides in/out per lattice cell, so a rib 1.3 cells thick still produces a legal, staircased HEX8 mesh. method="tet4" / "tet10" hand the dual-contour surface to TetGen as a piecewise linear complex (or to Gmsh, with mesher="gmsh", which sizes elements by the part rather than the lattice), and a PLC must be watertight, manifold and free of self-intersections. One QEF vertex per cell cannot represent two surface sheets passing through one cell, so where a wall is thinner than about two cells the extracted quads fold over each other and TetGen rejects the surface. method="cutfem" builds no volume mesh: the lattice’s cut cells are the discretization, and the dual-contour surface is extracted only to be drawn and selected on.
RuntimeError: TetGen rejected the surface: The input surface mesh contain
self-intersections. ...
Blends make this worse: a smooth union whose radius is comparable to the rib thickness folds the surface at the fillet even where the rib alone would mesh.

Refinement ladder
sdf_to_tet_mesh (and therefore SimMesh.build for the tet methods) walks a ladder of grids over the same box: the declared resolution, then ×1.5 and ×2.25, rounded up per axis. At every rung it tries sharp-feature placement first and the more robust Tikhonov placement second. Before each TetGen call the projected surface goes through self_intersections, so a rung already known to be folded is abandoned without paying for TetGen (the declared rung included). The first rung TetGen accepts wins, and the mesh’s grid is that rung, not the declared one.
The diagnostic is a sampled check: a hit proves the surface is folded, a miss proves nothing, and most rungs are settled by TetGen itself. It exists for the diagnosis, not for speed. On the end cap’s housing it costs 0.12–0.16 s a rung (145k–200k pairs), about 1% of the ~15 s of that rung’s extraction and projection but more than the 0.06–0.16 s TetGen takes to reject a folded surface. In exchange the rung is recorded as "self-intersecting" with a fold count instead of an opaque TetGen message.


Refinement record
Every mesh that came through the ladder carries a refinement record, and a SimulationResult re-exports it as result.refinement (with a digest under describe()["refinement"], None when nothing was refined). A plate with a blended rib two-thirds of a cell thick triggers it:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.fem import SimMesh
from cadjoint.sdf.boolean import Union
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box
from cadjoint.sdf.transforms import Translate

plate = Box([1.0, 1.0, 0.1])
rib = Translate(Box([0.12, 0.8, 0.4]), offset=jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.4]))
part = Union((plate, rib), smoothness=0.1)

sim_mesh = SimMesh(name="ribbed", resolution=(10, 10, 6), method="tet4",
                   bounds=(-1.1, -1.1, -0.2), size=(2.2, 2.2, 1.2))
mesh = sim_mesh.build(part)

record = mesh.refinement
print(record["declared"], "->", record["used"], record["refined"])
# (10, 10, 6) -> (15, 15, 9) True

for attempt in record["attempts"]:
    print(attempt["resolution"], attempt["sharp"], attempt["outcome"])
# (10, 10, 6)  True  self-intersecting
# (10, 10, 6)  False self-intersecting
# (15, 15, 9)  True  meshed
outcome is one of "meshed", "self-intersecting" (the diagnostic fired, TetGen was never run) or "rejected" (TetGen ran and refused; the attempt also carries "error"). A refined mesh is a different mesh (more nodes, more elements, a different frozen topology), so solves compared across designs should read used rather than assume the declared resolution.
max_refinements=0 (default 2) fails at the declared grid instead.


Refinement failures
If no rung works, the error names both ends of the ladder and the heuristic:
TetGen rejected the surface: ... The surface stays self-intersecting up to
(27, 27, 14) (declared (12, 12, 6), refined x1.5 and x2.25); the part likely
has features thinner than two cells at the declared resolution — raise the
declared resolution or use method='hex'.
Refinement fixes a surface that is only under-resolved. It does not fix a feature that is small in absolute terms. scenes/end_cap.py’s housing, measured over the ladder and well past it, it self-intersects at (26, 26, 13), (39, 39, 20), (59, 59, 30), (78, 78, 39), (104, 104, 52) and (130, 130, 65) alike. Only the kind of defect changes with resolution: at the declared (26, 26, 13) the surface is not even manifold (one edge shared by three triangles) and carries 48 folded triangle pairs; by (59, 59, 30) it is watertight and manifold, and still carries 16, all of them clustered on the snap-ring groove of the bearing seat (0.06 tall by 0.05 deep) and on the gusset-rib crests. Those two features are ~1.5 cells even at 2.25x. That part wants method="hex", a coarser blend, or a model change — not a finer grid.
sdf_to_tet_mesh Newton-projects the QEF vertices onto the zero set before tetrahedralizing, and on a coarse grid that projection can create folds: the same end-cap surface at (26, 26, 13) has 1 self-intersecting pair before projection and 48 after, because the projection clamp is half the cell diagonal and a vertex can be dragged across a thin wall. Refining shrinks the clamp with the cells, which is part of why the ladder works.


Boundary-vertex projection
A boundary vertex follows the design by being re-solved onto the model, and the result depends on which zero sets it is solved onto. Solved onto the scene’s single field, a vertex on a crease alternates between the two faces that meet there: its position wanders along the crease and its derivative is one face’s, not the edge’s. On the starter, measured in the cut-cell study, that affects 136 of 860 surface vertices and 11–13 % of the objective’s gradient.
A SimMesh therefore lowers its scene to the node table (cadjoint.zeroset), classifies each boundary vertex onto the census surfaces it lies on (one for a face, two for an edge, three at a corner), and moves it with the minimum-norm Newton solve on all of them at once (cadjoint.zeroset.project), the same solve the zero-set protocol’s Solve performs. The mesh motion, the viewer’s feature-edge seams and the tangent-plane constructor all call this one kernel.
A scene that cannot be lowered (a bare callable field) uses the single-field projection.

title: Meshing
text:
Gmsh
mesher selects what fills a tet4/tet10 mesh. The default, "tetgen", is everything above: the lattice sizes the elements and every node follows the design through recompute_tet_points. The example below is a plate with a through bore, a hard Difference with sharp edges:
from cadjoint.sdf.boolean import Difference
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Cylinder

plate = Difference((Box([0.6, 0.6, 0.4]), Cylinder(radius=0.25, height=0.9)),
                   smoothness=0.0)
mesh = SimMesh(name="plate", resolution=20, method="tet10", mesher="gmsh",
               bounds=(-0.83, -0.83, -0.63), size=(1.66, 1.66, 1.26))
mesher="gmsh" takes the same dual-contour surface, writes it as an STL, and hands it to Gmsh through the tet_mesher plugin. Gmsh’s classifySurfaces and createGeometry split the triangle soup into one reparametrised surface per smooth region, so it meshes a dozen faces of a part rather than three thousand facets; HXT fills the volume, and setOrder(2) puts the midside nodes on those surfaces rather than at chord midpoints. Differences from TetGen:

Element size is the part’s, not the lattice’s. The lattice is only how the surface was extracted; target_size (the grid’s smallest spacing by default) is what sizes the tets, and the refinement ladder does not run.
Quality is an order of magnitude better. At target_size=0.16 the plate’s worst radius ratio is 0.293 against the DC/TetGen path’s 0.04, with the median at 0.74.
Every node is tagged with the patches that own it. assign_ownership evaluates |f_p| on each Gmsh surface entity’s nodes for every patch of the scene’s decomposition and keeps the ones that clear the bar; the mesh carries the resulting OwnedNodes record.

built = mesh.build(plate)
built.mesher                      # 'gmsh'
built.owned.arity_counts()        # {0: 18281, 1: 9060, 2: 504, 3: 8}: 8 corners
built.stats["blend_surfaces"]     # 0: a hard CSG solid has no blend faces
Gmsh is GPL-2.0-or-later, so it is an optional extra (pip install 'cadjoint[gmsh]') or, in production, the cadjoint_tet_gmsh image where the licence boundary is a process boundary. Nothing under cadjoint/ imports it at module scope; see the tet_gmsh plugin.

Frozen geometry
A Gmsh mesh’s topology is decided once and held. Its positions follow the design through the node_map plugin kind (a per-arity Newton projection onto each node’s owning patches with the implicit-function adjoint, midsides re-solved on their own surfaces, interior nodes following by Laplacian relaxation), and nothing in this repository fills that kind; cadjoint.tier reports whether anything does.
Without it the mesh is frozen geometry: it builds, solves, inspects and exports like any other TetMesh, SimMesh.inspect() reports frozen_geometry: true, and an Optimization over a study on it is refused at declaration with one sentence naming the alternative. A one-field projection of every boundary node onto the scene’s zero set would produce a gradient, but it would take crease nodes off their creases and put midsides back on chords. mesher="tetgen", the default, is differentiable throughout.

title: Meshing
text:
Limitations

One QEF vertex per cell cannot represent two surface sheets crossing one cell face, so when a CSG seam grazes a lattice plane uniform dual contouring can emit nonmanifold edges. This is tracked as a strict xfail in tests/meshing/test_scenes.py and needs cell disambiguation.
Multi-size octree leaves (2:1 balancing, transition stitching) are not implemented.
Exports are faceted; an exact-surface STEP needs a step_export plugin.
A Gmsh mesh is frozen geometry unless a node_map plugin is installed.
