title: Optimization
text: An Optimization minimizes a scalar over the free parameters of a scene: a pure function of the parameters, or a declared simulation study. It returns the optimized parameters, the per-step history and a replayable trajectory; the viewer, the CLI and a script run the same object. The optimizer is optax, a core dependency.

title: Optimization
text:
Example
The objective form minimizes a pure function of the free parameters of a piece of geometry, with no simulation:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.geometry.parameters import Vector
from cadjoint.optimize import Optimization
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Sphere
from cadjoint.sdf.transforms import Translate

p = Vector([1.0, 1.0, 0.0], free=True, name="p")
scene = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.5), offset=p)

def objective(params):
    return jnp.sum(params["p"] ** 2)

run = Optimization(name="center", objective=objective, of=scene,
                   steps=40, learning_rate=0.1).run()

print(run.initial, "->", run.parameters)
# {'p': [1.0, 1.0, 0.0]} -> {'p': [0.1008, 0.1008, 0.0]}
print(run.history[0]["objective"], "->", run.objective)  # 2.0 -> 0.0203

title: Optimization
text:
Gradients
Every SDF is a pure JAX function, so jax.grad differentiates through geometry. Parameters can be passed as plain arrays:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.sdf import Sphere, Translate, Union, volume

def two_spheres(p1, p2):
    return Union(Translate(Sphere(radius=1.0), offset=p1),
                 Translate(Sphere(radius=1.0), offset=p2))

def loss(p1, p2):
    return volume(two_spheres(p1, p2))

value, (g1, g2) = jax.value_and_grad(loss, argnums=(0, 1))(
    jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), jnp.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
print(value, g1, g2)  # 6.873 [-1.891 0 0] [1.976 0 0]
volume integrates the SDF’s soft occupancy over a sampling box. Moving the spheres apart reduces their overlap, so the union’s volume grows along ±x.
Explicit arguments scale poorly once a scene has many parameters spread over its tree. Tagging parameters free=True on the geometry lets extract_parameters collect them, and functionalize turns the tree into a function of the parameter dictionaries:
from cadjoint import extract_parameters, functionalize
from cadjoint.geometry import Vector

p1 = Vector(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="p1")
p2 = Vector(jnp.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="p2")
scene = Union(Translate(Sphere(radius=1.0), offset=p1),
              Translate(Sphere(radius=1.0), offset=p2))

free, fixed, metadata = extract_parameters(scene)
sdf = functionalize(scene)

value, grads = jax.value_and_grad(lambda params: volume(sdf(params, fixed)))(free)
print(grads)  # {'p1': [-1.891, 0, 0], 'p2': [1.976, 0, 0]}
extract_parameters returns three dictionaries: free parameter values keyed by name, fixed values keyed by tree path (union_0.smoothness, sphere_2.radius, …), and metadata holding the Parameter object behind each free value. functionalize(scene)(free, fixed) is a callable point → distance; the tree structure is fixed when it is built and the parameter values vary. Both forms give the same gradient. With parameter extraction, any node can declare a parameter free without changing the loss or the optimizer. Modelling covers parameters, functionalize and functionalize_parametric in full.

title: Optimization
text:
Objective and study forms
An Optimization takes one of two mutually exclusive forms: the objective form of the example, and the study form, which makes a declared ThermalStudy or ElasticStudy the objective, differentiating through geometry → mesh → solve → scalar:
from cadjoint.fem import Dirichlet, HeatFlux, Nodes, SimMesh, ThermalStudy
from cadjoint.geometry.parameters import Vector
from cadjoint.optimize import Optimization
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box

bar = Box(Vector([1.0, 0.15, 0.15], free=True, name="size"))
mesh = SimMesh(name="bar-mesh", resolution=(22, 5, 5),
               bounds=(-1.1, -0.25, -0.25), size=(2.2, 0.5, 0.5))
study = ThermalStudy(
    name="bar-conduction",
    conductivity=2.0,
    bcs=[Dirichlet(Nodes.side("+x"), 0.0), HeatFlux(Nodes.side("-x"), 4.0)],
    mesh=mesh,
)

def volume(params):
    s = params["size"]
    return 8.0 * s[0] * s[1] * s[2]

run = Optimization(
    name="cool-bar",
    study=study,
    metric="max",
    regularizer=volume,
    regularizer_weight=0.1,
    steps=3,
    learning_rate=0.01,
    remesh_every=0,
).run(scene=bar)

print(run.history[0]["objective"], "->", run.objective)  # 4.018 -> 2.964
print(run.parameters)  # {'size': [0.970, 0.180, 0.179]}
Three Adam steps thicken the bar and lower peak temperature from 4.018 to 2.964; the volume penalty keeps it from growing without limit.
study= also accepts the name of a study, as scene files use it. Names resolve only inside a capture_studies() context, which the playground opens when it executes a scene; a standalone script passes the study instance.
Mixing the forms is refused: metric, regularizer, remesh_every, and a non-direct gradient_path all belong to the study form, and objective / of are rejected alongside study.

title: Optimization
text:
Metrics
metric reduces the solved field to one number.








metric
ObjectiveMetric
Means




"mean"
ObjectiveMetric.MEAN
The mean of the field — temperature, or displacement magnitude


"max"
ObjectiveMetric.MAX
Its maximum


"compliance"
ObjectiveMetric.COMPLIANCE
The work of the applied loads, f·u (twice the strain energy)



Every fixed option on Optimization has an enum in cadjoint.enums (ObjectiveMetric, GradientPath, OptimizerMethod with "adam" / "sgd"), and the member and the string are interchangeable.
"compliance" requires an elastic study with at least one Traction boundary condition; without loads the declaration is rejected.
The starter scene’s heat sink minimizes "max": the die is the hot spot, and a mean-temperature objective rewards deleting hot material instead of cooling the chip.
regularizer is a function of the parameters, added as objective + regularizer_weight * regularizer(params) and differentiated in reverse mode with the objective. In the starter scene it is a smoothed material volume computed by evaluating the traced SDF on a lattice.

title: Optimization
text:
Constrained optimization
Every update is projected back onto the constraint manifold. When extract_parameters reports a non-empty residual for the scene’s parameters, the optimizer chains a Newton projection after the optimizer transform:
import optax
from cadjoint import extract_parameters
from cadjoint.constraints import DistanceConstraint
from cadjoint.constraints.solve import make_manifold_projection
from cadjoint.geometry.parameters import Vector
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Sphere
from cadjoint.sdf.transforms import Translate

p = Vector([2.0, 0.0, 0.0], free=True, name="p")
anchor = Vector([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], free=False, name="anchor")
DistanceConstraint(p, anchor, 2.0)
scene = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.5), offset=p)
free, fixed, metadata = extract_parameters(scene)

transform = optax.chain(optax.adam(0.1),
                        make_manifold_projection(metadata, steps=2))
Optimization does this automatically. Horizontals stay horizontal and pinned dimensions stay pinned; the optimizer moves only within the sketch’s remaining degrees of freedom.
The same descent can be written by hand. The block below minimizes ‖p − target‖² subject to |p| = 2 from p₀ = (2, 0, 0) with target (1, 1.5, 0), whose optimum is p* = target · 2/|target| ≈ (1.109, 1.664, 0) at loss 0.0389, using five strategies for 40 steps each:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax
from cadjoint import extract_parameters
from cadjoint.constraints import (
    DistanceConstraint, constraint_residuals, make_manifold_projection, null_space,
)
from cadjoint.geometry import Vector

anchor = Vector(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
p = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="p")
constraint = DistanceConstraint(anchor, p, distance=2.0)
free, fixed, metadata = extract_parameters(constraint)

target = jnp.array([1.0, 1.5, 0.0])
p_star = target * (2.0 / jnp.linalg.norm(target))       # optimum: (1.109, 1.664, 0)

def objective(params):
    return jnp.sum((params["p"] - target) ** 2)

value_and_grad = jax.value_and_grad(objective)

N0 = null_space(free, metadata)                          # tangent basis at the start
def grad_fixed(params):                                  # 1. fixed null space
    value, g = jax.value_and_grad(lambda z: objective(N0 @ z))(params @ N0)
    return value, N0 @ g

def grad_relin(params):                                  # 2./4. current null space
    N = null_space(params, metadata)
    value, g = value_and_grad(params)
    return value, N @ (g @ N)

LAMBDA = 25.0
def grad_penalty(params):                                # 5. penalty
    penalty = lambda q: objective(q) + LAMBDA * jnp.sum(constraint_residuals(q, metadata) ** 2)
    return objective(params), jax.grad(penalty)(params)

strategies = {
    "fixed null-space": (grad_fixed, optax.adam(0.05)),
    "relinearized null-space": (grad_relin, optax.sgd(0.15)),
    "manifold projection": (value_and_grad,
                            optax.chain(optax.adam(0.05), make_manifold_projection(metadata))),
    "Riemannian GD": (grad_relin,
                      optax.chain(optax.sgd(0.15), make_manifold_projection(metadata))),
    "penalty": (grad_penalty, optax.adam(2.5 / (1.0 + 2.0 * LAMBDA))),
}

for label, (grad_fn, opt) in strategies.items():
    params, state = free, opt.init(free)
    for _ in range(40):
        value, g = grad_fn(params)
        updates, state = opt.update(g, state, params)    # params= activates the projection
        params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)
    violation = jnp.linalg.norm(constraint_residuals(params, metadata))
    print(f"{label:24s} loss {float(objective(params)):.4f}  |r| {float(violation):.1e}")
fixed null-space         loss 1.0000  |r| 5.0e-01
relinearized null-space  loss 0.1097  |r| 1.3e-01
manifold projection      loss 0.0392  |r| 1.2e-07
Riemannian GD            loss 0.0389  |r| 0.0e+00
penalty                  loss 0.0450  |r| 8.4e-03










Strategy
Step
Cost per step
Constraint after each step
Use when




Fixed null-space
Gradient projected onto N Nᵀ, N = null_space(...) computed once at x₀
One gradient; N reused
Drifts: the step follows the tangent plane at x₀, not at the current point
Linear constraints, where the tangent plane does not rotate


Relinearized null-space
N recomputed at the current point, gradient projected onto the current tangent plane
One gradient plus one null_space
Drifts by O(lr²κ) per step, with no correction
A cheap manifold-aware direction, followed by a projection


Manifold projection
optax.chain(opt, make_manifold_projection(metadata))
One gradient plus a Newton correction
Exact
Any optax optimizer; what Optimization uses


Riemannian GD
Relinearized direction, then make_manifold_projection
One gradient, one null_space, a Newton correction
Exact
Tangent-plane direction with exact feasibility; reached the optimum here


Penalty
Loss ‖p − t‖² + λ‖r(p)‖²
One gradient
Approximate, error shrinks as λ grows
No projection available; soft constraints



make_manifold_projection(metadata) computes params + update from the chained optimizer, projects it onto the constraint manifold with a Newton correction, and returns projected − params as the effective update, so optax.apply_updates(params, updates) lands on the manifold. It needs the current parameters: opt.update(grads, state, params) activates it, and standard optax transforms ignore the extra argument.
Relinearized steps use plain SGD rather than Adam: as the null space rotates, components that were zero acquire non-zero projections, and Adam’s element-wise scaling amplifies them and pushes the step off the tangent plane.
The penalty’s Hessian eigenvalue in the normal direction is 2 + 2λ, so a stable learning rate is at most 1/(1 + 2λ).

title: Optimization
text:
Frozen topology
Meshing has a discrete half (which cells are inside, how they connect) and a continuous half (where the nodes sit). Only the continuous half is differentiable, so the optimizer freezes topology and differentiates through node positions: each step re-projects the boundary nodes onto the current design’s zero set, Newton-corrected against the true SDF, with total motion clamped to half a cell diagonal.
remesh_every (default 6; 0 disables it) re-extracts the mesh at the current design every that many steps. The objective jumps at those steps are the discretization changing: on the bracket the step-12 re-extraction raised the objective from 6.02 to 8.86 and the step-18 one lowered it from 7.99 to 5.53, because the web is about two cells thick and a one-cell change in the loaded wall changes the discrete compliance substantially.
The final reported objective is evaluated on a freshly extracted mesh, so it does not depend on the last frozen topology.
A frozen topology also fixes every array shape, so the objective is compiled once per topology with jax.jit and each step costs a solve rather than a re-trace. On the starter scene this takes a step from ~11 s to 0.5–0.8 s, with the objective identical to 13 digits (performance notes).

title: Optimization
text:
Gradient paths
gradient_path selects which stages run outside JAX.








Value
GradientPath
Chain




"direct" (default)
GradientPath.DIRECT
Everything in-process. Node positions re-projected onto the true SDF, solved by the chosen backend.


"tesseract"
GradientPath.TESSERACT
Lattice samples → mesher Tesseract → solver Tesseract. Meshes the trilinear interpolant, so the gradient carries only normal boundary motion.


"tesseract-dc"
GradientPath.TESSERACT_DC
Dual contouring stays in JAX on the true SDF; only TetGen is wrapped, by the tetfill Tesseract with its exact pass-through VJP. Tet meshes only.



"tesseract-dc" keeps dual contouring in JAX against the true field, which preserves fin creases; the starter scene declares it. Both Tesseract paths need the tesseract extra. Whichever path runs the descent, the final result is evaluated on the direct path.
The stages behind both paths are plugins resolved by kind (mesher, tetfill, thermal_solver, elastic_solver), so where each runs is configuration. The plugins page gives the cost of each boundary.

title: Optimization
text:
Run results
run() returns an OptimizationRun:

history — one {"step", "objective", "grad_norm"} record per step, at the parameters before that step’s update. A non-finite objective or gradient norm aborts rather than propagating NaNs.
trajectory — {"step", "objective", "parameters"}, subsampled to at most 100 entries with the first and last always kept. This is what the viewer’s scrubber replays.
initial and parameters — before and after.
objective — the final objective.
result — the concrete SimulationResult from the final evaluation (study form only).

run(callback=fn) receives each history record as it is produced; the playground streams progress this way. method is "adam" or "sgd"; without optax it degrades to plain gradient descent and reports "gradient-descent".
Study runs execute inside an x64 scope, promote parameters to float64, and restore the target’s original parameter values on exit — including on failure.



A finished cool-sink run in the playground: the Results window replays the trajectory with its objective sparkline and scrubber (step 2 of 8), beside the Optimize window’s step count and learning rate

title: Optimization
text:
Bracket example
examples/fem_bracket_optimization.py runs the full loop on the parametric L-bracket from scenes/bracket.py: three named CAD parameters (web_thickness, rib_height, plate_thickness) → bracket SDF → HEX8 mesh → linear elastic solve → compliance plus mass → Adam with box-bound projection.
uv run python examples/fem_bracket_optimization.py            # ~10 min, CPU
uv run python examples/fem_bracket_optimization.py --smoke    # 2 cheap steps
uv run python examples/fem_bracket_optimization.py --backend calculix
Over 30 steps the objective falls 17.44 → 4.69, a 73% reduction; compliance drops 81% while mass rises 27%. The adjoint is validated against central differences at the initial design to 2.3e-5, 2.0e-3, and 3.3e-7 relative on the three parameters. --backend calculix runs CalculiX (Fortran) inside the same jax.grad call without changing the objective. Convergence CSV, a figure, and before/after VTK files land in examples/output/. The run record has the measured run, the rationale for the box bounds, and a known CalculiX deck fragility.

title: Rendering
text: cadjoint.render draws an SDF scene to an (H, W, 3) float array with early-exit sphere tracing, finite-difference normals, Cook–Torrance GGX materials, soft shadows and optional reflection and refraction. The same scene compiles through StableHLO to a WGSL shader that the interactive viewer renders live.

title: Rendering
text:
Example
from cadjoint.render import Camera, RenderSettings, Scene, render_scene
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Sphere

scene = Scene(
    Sphere(1.0),
    camera=Camera(position=(0, 1.5, 5), target=(0, 0, 0)),
)
image = render_scene(scene, RenderSettings.balanced((240, 320)))
print(image.shape)   # (240, 320, 3)

title: Rendering
text:
Scene
Scene holds the geometry, the camera, the lights and the environment. light_directions and light_colors are matched tuples, one entry per light; make_gradient_sky builds an environment map from three colours.
from cadjoint.render import Material, make_gradient_sky
from cadjoint.sdf.boolean import Union
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Plane, Torus
from cadjoint.sdf.transforms import Rotate, Translate

geometry = Union(
    Translate(Sphere(0.82, material=Material(color=[0.78, 0.06, 0.03], roughness=0.42)),
              [-1.45, -0.10, 0.0]),
    Translate(Rotate(Torus(0.62, 0.23, material=Material(color=[1.0, 0.58, 0.08],
                                                          roughness=0.28, metallic=0.8)),
                     axis="y", angle=0.45),
              [0.0, -0.07, 0.0]),
    Plane(-0.92, material=Material(color=[0.10, 0.12, 0.16], roughness=0.72)),
    smoothness=0.0,
)
lit = Scene(
    geometry,
    camera=Camera(position=(4.4, 3.5, 7.5), target=(0.0, -0.35, 0.0), fov=0.38),
    light_directions=((0.35, 1.0, 0.55), (-0.65, 0.45, -0.2)),
    light_colors=((1.5, 1.35, 1.15), (0.22, 0.3, 0.5)),
    environment_map=make_gradient_sky(
        sky_color=(0.7, 0.76, 0.88),
        horizon_color=(0.18, 0.27, 0.44),
        ground_color=(0.16, 0.18, 0.24),
    ),
)
image = render_scene(lit, RenderSettings.balanced((180, 240)))
The low-level raymarch(sdf, ...) takes the geometry and the settings as keyword arguments; render_raymarched(...) wraps it to draw on a matplotlib axis.

text:
Quality presets
RenderSettings sets the performance/fidelity trade-off, separately from the scene.

draft is direct lighting with no secondary visibility. balanced adds soft shadows and reconstructed silhouettes. high_quality tightens surface precision and doubles the shadow budget. Reflection and refraction are off in all three.



Draft, balanced, and high-quality forward renders


Presets are immutable dataclasses. Every field is public and validated; override one with dataclasses.replace:
from dataclasses import replace

mirror = replace(RenderSettings.balanced(), reflect_steps=64)
A primary ray stops at the first hit or at max_distance, so a direct hit uses a small fraction of max_steps and a miss does not evaluate the field for every step. Soft-shadow rays stop at the first occluder.
Each primary trace keeps its closest approach to the scene. A ray that narrowly misses a surface receives screen-space coverage across silhouette_smoothing pixels, which removes hard hit/miss outlines. Set it to 0 for exact binary coverage.

title: Rendering
text:
Compilation and caching
The first render_scene call includes JAX compilation. The renderer is one module-level jax.jit: the scene tree, the image shape and the step counts (max_steps, shadow_steps, reflect_steps, refract_steps) are static, and the design parameter values are traced inputs. A later call that changes only parameter values, the camera or the lights reuses the compiled program; a new preset or resolution compiles once more.
from time import perf_counter

settings = RenderSettings.balanced((128, 160))
render_scene(lit, settings)               # compiles
start = perf_counter()
render_scene(lit, settings)               # cached
print(f"{(perf_counter() - start) * 1e3:.1f} ms")

title: Rendering
text:
Materials
Attach a Material to any primitive. It is queried per hit point, and Union blends materials across a smooth boundary.
sphere = Sphere(
    radius=1.0,
    material=Material(
        color=[0.22, 0.50, 0.95],
        roughness=0.35,
        metallic=0.0,
        opacity=1.0,
        ior=1.0,
    ),
)



Direct lighting, soft shadows, metal reflections, and glass refraction



Transparency and refraction
opacity < 1 makes a surface transparent. With refract_steps=0 (the default) it fades toward the background. With refract_steps > 0 the renderer refracts twice by Snell’s law: the primary ray bends into the material, an interior march finds the back face using −sdf as the distance field, and the ray bends back into air. Schlick–Fresnel brightens the rim at grazing angles.
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.render import raymarch

glass = Sphere(radius=1.0, material=Material(
    color=[0.92, 0.97, 1.0], roughness=0.05, opacity=0.04, ior=1.5))
red_ball = Translate(
    Sphere(radius=0.65, material=Material(color=[0.93, 0.26, 0.22])),
    offset=jnp.array([-1.1, 0.5, -3.0]),
)

image = raymarch(
    Union((glass, red_ball), smoothness=0.0),
    camera_pos=jnp.array([0.0, 0.5, 5.5]),
    resolution=(200, 200),
    background_color=jnp.array([0.07, 0.09, 0.16]),
    refract_steps=48,
    max_steps=80,
    aa_samples=2,
)

title: Rendering
text:
Shader compilation
A scene compiles to a standalone WGSL shader. JAX traces distance and material evaluation and lowers both to StableHLO, from which cadjoint emits the shader source, so the browser renders the same field as the Python renderer:
JAX scene → jax.export → StableHLO MLIR → WGSL → WebGPU fragment shader
from cadjoint.backends import compile_scene_to_wgsl, compile_sdf_to_wgsl

wgsl = compile_sdf_to_wgsl(Sphere(radius=1.0))          # `fn sdf` only
scene_wgsl = compile_scene_to_wgsl(Sphere(radius=1.0))  # + materials
print(wgsl[:200])
compile_scene_to_wgsl emits sdf, material_base (RGB + roughness) and material_optics (metallic + opacity + IOR + reflectivity) from one scene snapshot. The whole tree becomes one WGSL function per entry point; the GPU evaluates the field directly, with no intermediate mesh. The playground compiles on every run.

Shader size
A shader is one straight-line function per entry point, so its size depends on how much of the tree the trace unrolls. A node evaluated more than once (a pattern’s child, a subtree two booleans share) is lowered as its own StableHLO function, which the emitter turns into one WGSL function called per instance; a bearing housing with four polar patterns is 1.45 MB of WGSL rather than 2.42 MB. The vertex loop of a sketch profile is not shared: WGSL has no type wider than a mat4, so a profile’s vertices stay individual vec2s and its contribution grows with the vertex count. Everything else traces the profile as one (N, 2) array; see program size.


Uniform parameters
Design parameters are inlined as float literals by default, so editing one rewrites the module and the browser recompiles it. uniforms=True returns a ShaderProgram: the same source for every parameter value, plus a vec4-per-parameter uniform layout.
from cadjoint.geometry import Scalar

sized = Sphere(radius=Scalar(1.0, free=True, name="radius"))
program = compile_scene_to_wgsl(sized, uniforms=True)
program.wgsl                 # identical across every value edit
program.parameters[0].name   # 'radius', the name extract_parameters uses
program.buffer()             # float32 array to upload at @group(3) @binding(0)

title: Rendering
text:
Limitations

Rendered pixels are not differentiable: visibility carries no gradient, and the renderer is not an inverse-rendering or optimization interface. Gradients run through meshing and simulation.

title: Playground
text: The playground is a local browser application with a Python editor, a WebGPU viewport, and windows that edit the program in the editor. The program holds all state. Every edit in the UI — dragging a sketch vertex, adding a boundary condition, accepting an optimized design — rewrites literals in the source, and every window is rebuilt from the next compile. Geometry whose literals cannot be rewritten (built in a loop, or from a variable) renders but is read-only.

title: Playground
text:
Starting the server
The playground ships in the cadjoint package as cadjoint-viewer. It needs the viewer extra; editor adds lint, completion and signature help.
uvx --from "cadjoint[viewer,editor]" cadjoint-viewer --open   # no checkout, no environment
pip install "cadjoint[viewer,editor]" && cadjoint-viewer --open
From a checkout:
uv sync --extra viewer --extra editor
uv run cadjoint-viewer --open                 # serves http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and opens a browser
uv run python -m cadjoint.viewer.playground   # same server, no browser launch
uv run cadjoint-viewer --port 9000            # another port; --help lists the flags
Scenes open from and save to ./scenes under the directory the server was started in, or CADJOINT_SCENES_DIR. In a checkout that is the example scenes; elsewhere it starts empty. The playground opens on a built-in starter, a parametric heat sink: a fin comb extruded from one constrained sketch, a revolved copper slug under the die, two steel bushings, and a declared mesh, thermal study and optimization. The viewport needs a WebGPU-capable browser. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.






Warning



The playground executes the editor contents as Python on your computer. It binds only to localhost, protects requests with a per-session token, and compiles each edit in a timed child process so a failing edit cannot take the server down — but it is not a sandbox. Only run code you trust.

text:
Modelling

Tools
The tool rail floats in the viewport’s top-left corner. A group button shows its last-used tool; hover or click opens a flyout of the rest. At 1280 px and wider each button carries its word. A tool that cannot act says why in its tooltip (Extrude — select a sketch first).

Sketch, Sketch on face, Point; in Model also Box, Sphere, Cylinder
K, —, P, B S C

Distance, Horizontal, Vertical, Coincident, Parallel, Perpendicular, Fix
—

Removes the selection
⌫



One tool is armed at a time; finishing or cancelling it returns to Select.

Sketch places a new sketch on the plane chosen in the rail’s plane row (XY, YZ, ZX, or Face); a ghost shows where it lands.
Point inserts a vertex wherever you click a sketch edge, until Esc.
Box / Sphere / Cylinder write a Solid.* call where you click.
Loft waits for a click on a second sketch with the same vertex count.
Distance, Horizontal, Vertical, Coincident take two sketch points; Parallel, Perpendicular two edges; Fix anchors the selected point.
The gizmo’s arrows and rings rewrite position=, rotation= or the size arguments; Scale needs a solid primitive.



Selecting and editing
A click selects; the viewport, Objects, Properties and the editor show the same selection, and the editor scrolls to its source without taking focus. A vertex selection highlights its exact literal. Click empty space, or Esc, to clear.
A free sketch point — a parameter the optimizer may move — is a hollow blue ring and the solid follows the drag live; a held point is a filled ink square and the solid catches up after release and a recompile; the selected point is a filled circle. Hovering a handle names it in the hint. A drag writes the source once, on release, as one undo step; Esc during the drag puts the value back.
Objects is the read-only tree of the scene: sketches with their point counts and the features built from them, primitives with their dimensions, each with its material. Booleans nest their operands, an object used twice appears again as a reference, an unnamed boolean reads “Union of a, b…”, and objects the scene does not use collect under “Not in scene”. Clicking a feature row (EXTRUDE line 154) points Properties at it.
Properties lists the arguments the selected element was written with. Literal numbers and vectors are fields, a material is a dropdown of the program’s materials, and anything written as an expression is shown as written, read-only. A field commits on Enter or blur, keeps its written precision, and shows its unit beside it. When Properties shows a tree row rather than the selection, follow selection returns it to the viewport’s selection.
Sketch shows the selected sketch’s constraints as chips (distance · P1–P2 = 1.8 ×): a distance’s number is editable, × (or ⌫ on a selected chip) removes one. Its buttons are Fix, Extrude, Revolve, Loft and Solver, which runs the constraint solver (Newton projection, Adam or SGD, for a chosen iteration count) and plots its residual.



Sketch mode with the fin comb selected: the move gizmo on the sketch plane, Properties showing the sketch and its plane, and the Sketch window listing fix, distance, horizontal, vertical and equal constraints




Sketch on face
Sketch on face writes a reference to the face, not its current coordinates: SketchPlane.on(body.cap("+")), SketchPlane.on(block.face("+z")), or, on a curved surface with no face to name, SketchPlane.tangent(body, near=[...]). Re-dimension the parent and the sketch moves with it, and gradients downstream still reach the parent’s parameters — see faces as references. In Model it starts a new sketch; in Sketch it re-plants the selected one. A face whose feature is not bound to a variable has no name in the source, and the hint says so. A sketch can only sit on geometry built before it.


Undo and Escape
Undo (⌘Z, ⇧⌘Z to redo) steps through source versions: each run, patch and drag is one step; inside the editor it is the editor’s own history. Removing an object, constraint, study, boundary condition, mesh or optimization is not confirmed — the toolbar shows removed … Undo ⌘Z instead.
Esc cancels one thing per press, most specific first: a drag in flight, a half-finished command (a constraint’s second pick, a loft’s second sketch), the armed tool, the selection, then the mode. With nothing left it does nothing.

Materials
Materials shows a swatch per Material in the program and how many objects use it. Drag a swatch onto an object in the viewport to assign it; Properties’ material dropdown does the same. + (or Model › Create › Material) declares a new one.
The inspector has two sections. Appearance — colour, roughness, metallic, opacity — uses a colour picker and sliders. Physical is what the solver reads, in SI, with the unit beside each field: a stated property is a field with × to remove it, an unstated one a state button that writes the keyword into the call. A property written as an expression is shown and not edited.
Values are held to the same brackets Material enforces with free=True, so a number the inspector accepts is one the optimizer accepts. A refusal appears under its row and names the unit — `density` must be a number from 1 to 25000 kg/m^3.

The refusal offers Write it out as a Material(…), which rewrites the binding as the literal call, one keyword per line, and then applies the edit. Only a bare, argument-free factory call is converted, so the server never runs your code to do it.
Under the hood every edit is one set_material_property patch, naming the material and carrying the property and a number, or null to remove it:
{"op": "set_material_property", "id": "assign:copper",

title: Playground
text:
Simulating
Meshes, Studies, Results and Optimize edit the declarations a script reads; the Simulate menu reaches them from any mode. Every option they offer — mesh method, study kind, boundary-condition type, objective — is one of the cadjoint.enums option sets.
Meshes has a card per SimMesh: resolution, padding, bounds, size, domain, and the method — Hex, Tet4, Tet10, or Cut cells (thermal studies only, solved by CutFEM on the lattice). Generate mesh builds it, reports node and element counts, and shades it by element quality with a histogram. A tet mesh that had to climb the refinement ladder says which grid it was built on. With no SimMesh declared, the window offers to generate a study’s implicit mesh.
Studies has a card per study: its coefficients, its mesh and domain as dropdowns, its boundary conditions, and Solve (which becomes Stop while it runs). + Boundary condition opens a builder: a type, a selection (Side, Box, Sphere, Half-space) and a value. Pick in viewport arms the viewport: a click on the mesh proposes a Nodes.sphere sized from the mesh spacing, a ⇧-drag a Nodes.box around the vertices inside the rectangle. The proposal only fills the builder; Add writes it into the program as a selection expression that re-resolves against whatever the mesh becomes. Hovering a BC row paints its nodes on the mesh. A study without conductivity= (or youngs= / poisson=) takes the property from the scene’s materials.



Simulate mode: the Studies window with the sink-conduction thermal study, its heat-flux and fixed-value boundary conditions and the Solve button; Results below is empty


Results shows the solved field in the viridis ramp, which nothing else in the app uses. Its controls: a field picker that swaps scalars without re-solving, the min / mean / max table, View mesh quality, Deformed with a warp scale for elastic results, Scene / Mesh to switch the viewport between the raymarched scene and the mesh, Element edges, and an axis-aligned Slice. Clicking the field probes the nearest vertex. A result whose source has since changed is kept and marked stale · source changed.



The solved sink-conduction temperature field in Results, with its legend, field table and X slice; Scenes, Studies, Meshes and Processes are open around a narrowed viewport


Optimize has a card per Optimization: its objective, steps and learning rate, Run and Stop. While it runs, the card shows the step, the time per step and the objective so far. A finished run writes the optimized literals into the source and opens a player — a convergence sparkline, play/pause and a scrubber (← →) — that replays the geometry along the trajectory by ghost-compiling each step’s parameters; only the final source enters undo history. A study-backed run also lands in Results, showing the optimized design’s field.



The cool-sink optimization replaying at step 2 of 8 in Results, over a stale temperature field; the Optimize card with its steps and learning rate is on the right

Render settings
Render, in the viewport bar (also View › Render › Settings…), opens the render popover in any mode. It holds three editable presets — X-Ray for modelling, Studio for path-traced materials, Wire for construction only — stored in the browser; Customize opens the settings under the selected preset, with Save and Reset.

Distance-field views
All five views are branches of the one generated shader, reading the same sdf() the solid is traced from.







View
Shows




Solid
The raymarched surface

The signed field on a plane, inside and out, with isolines at the grid spacing and a fifth of it; the section outline is the f = 0 contour


∇f
|∇f| on the same plane: 1 where the field is a true distance, anything else where a blend, scale or twist has broken that

The slice plane takes any axis and sweeps ±2 units; its coordinate and the contour intervals print beside the grid readout. Capped section cuts the solid on the same plane and closes the cut with a face. The offset slider traces f = c instead of f = 0 for every ray, shadow and normal; a positive offset dilates the part and a negative one erodes it, which checks a wall thickness or a clearance.



The distance-field slice on the X plane through the heat sink, contoured from inside to outside, with its legend and the SLICE X readout under the grid readout




Feature edges and wireframe
Both overlays come from one dual-contouring of the scene on the viewport’s 64³ grid. Mesh wireframe draws its quads. Feature edges draws the sharp layer: cells classified as creases, corners or exact min/max CSG seams, linked into chains, with seam vertices Newton-projected onto the intersection of the operands. The overlay cannot beat its grid: a bore rim is a polygon, and a fillet smaller than a cell is drawn as the sharp edge it rounds. The feature_edges plugin kind traces curves exactly instead; the compile payload says which source drew them (lattice or graph).



Feature edges drawn over the heat sink’s creases and seams, with a mesh job counting in the toolbar’s job chip




B-rep inspector
B-rep inspector replaces the solid with the B-rep the private tier derived (the brep plugin kind), on the same 64³ grid, so an extraction can be judged by eye. Each face is drawn from the extraction’s own tessellation in a categorical colour that no neighbour shares. Edges are stroked by kind: traced and sampled are the curves the feature-edge overlay draws, and every other boundary chain the graph built keeps its own state (blend, tangent, coincident, …, or undrawn for a crossing the overlay dropped). A kind the viewer has no tone for is drawn in grey under its own name. Vertices are dots.
The card in the top-left corner gives the counts and the path. That is Exact · analytic, or the dual-contouring fallback with the reason the exact path refused. Hovering a face shows its id, surface type (plane, cylinder, sphere, cone, blend or faceted) and owning patch. Hovering an edge shows its faces and how far it lies off the solid. Hovering a vertex shows its position. Highlight off-surface marks the edges whose points sit more than a tenth of a cell off the scene’s zero set, which is how a curve under a smooth blend gives itself away. Each legend row is a switch that hides its kind.
The B-rep is requested lazily through POST /api/brep and only while the inspector is on. Without diff-brep the switch is greyed out with the reason; when the extraction raises, the card prints the exception and the frame it came from, and the solid stays on screen.


Public and private tier
The exact paths are part of the private tier (diff-brep): the derived B-rep, its edge curves, analytic STEP, and the node map that lets a Gmsh mesh follow the design. Without diff-brep each of these features still runs, on dual contouring, and the viewer labels it where you choose it. A small chip says what you get and where it comes from: Feature edges reads Approximate · lattice and the STEP entry in File › Export… reads STEP · faceted. B-rep inspector is disabled, and a Gmsh mesh in the Meshes window reads Frozen geometry · public tier. A dashed chip edge marks the public form, and one line under the control gives the reason. With diff-brep the same chips read Exact … · private tier. The viewer reads all of this once from GET /api/capabilities, and the wording comes from cadjoint.tier, which the library’s own refusals also use. To see the public tier on a machine with diff-brep installed, start the playground with CADJOINT_PUBLIC_TIER=1.

Scenes and Processes
Scenes (File › Open…, ⌘O) browses the scenes directory. Each card shows a thumbnail, the first paragraph of the file’s docstring, size and date, and counts of parameters (named and free), studies, meshes and optimizations, with the materials it defines. Everything but the thumbnail is read with ast; no file is executed to describe it. Thumbnails render one at a time from each scene’s compiled shader and are cached. Refresh re-reads the directory. Opening a scene replaces the editor (an unsaved buffer asks first). File › Save (⌘S) and Save As… (⇧⌘S) write into the same directory, which accepts bare *.py names only. Running shows each job’s elapsed time, CPU and memory, with a cancel; History lists what finished, and clicking a solve, inspection or optimization reopens its result in the window that draws it; Load shows totals, worker CPU over the last minute, the result store’s budget, and Clear. title: Playground
text:
Server internals
Compilation. Each run evaluates the program in a fresh child process and reads scene. cadjoint walks the SDF graph and writes the WGSL functions sdf, material_base and material_optics directly; the browser embeds them in the preview or path-tracing runtime and builds the pipelines. A profile’s vertices are buffer slots and a pattern is a loop, so the module stays small. CADJOINT_SHADER_FORM=traced selects the JAX/StableHLO backend, tested point for point against the direct one; a shape the direct backend has no kernel for falls back to it and says so. Help › Developer › Show generated WGSL shows the module. Python tracebacks and WGSL errors appear under the editor.
Caching. The worker uses JAX’s persistent compilation cache under ~/.cache/cadjoint/jax (CADJOINT_CACHE_DIR moves it, CADJOINT_NO_COMPILATION_CACHE=1 disables it), and traces parameters as arguments, so a re-dimensioned design hits the cache; on the starter scene a warm solve takes 3.1 s against 14.3 s cold (benchmarks/jax_compile_profile.py). The server warms the cache for the scene it opens. See program size and the performance notes.
Source patches. Every edit is a /api/patch request that rewrites a span of the source; there are 28 operations. Each addressable thing carries a stable id derived from its AST path and the name the program gave it — assign:comb_profile, call:extrude@comb_profile, box:block, bc:sink-conduction[1], face:sink:cap+ — so an edit elsewhere in the file cannot redirect a patch; only an object with neither a variable nor a name= falls back to an ordinal #<n>.
The contract. Every request and response of every route, and every message between the server and its worker process, is a pydantic model in cadjoint/viewer/schema/; api.ROUTES lists the routes. The server checks each worker reply against its model before a route answers (a mismatch comes back as error_kind: "contract" rather than reaching the browser), and the frontend’s types are generated from the same models into payloads.d.ts (python -m cadjoint.viewer.schema.emit). The contract is versioned: GET /api/session reports api_version, every response carries it in X-Cadjoint-Api, and a page built for another version says so instead of misreading the server. tests/viewer/test_parity_roundtrip.py checks that every operation’s result parses, is deterministic and shows exactly the requested change, and that every set_* is idempotent.
Scene graph. The compile payload carries the scene as a version 2 cadjoint-scene graph (scene_graph, specified in cadjoint/backends/jaxjs/SCENE_FORMAT.md) next to the WGSL built from it. frontend/src/scene builds the same shaders from the graph in the browser, byte for byte. The server’s shaders are drawn by default. With ?shaders=browser in the URL, or localStorage["cadjoint.shaders"] = "browser", the page draws its own, and falls back to the server’s with a console warning when their shader_hash differs. frontend/static.html uses only the graph: it draws and exports the bundled scenes with no server.
Jobs. Every request that takes real time is registered as a job with a job_id and the sha256 of the source it ran on. GET /api/jobs lists jobs and live CPU/RSS totals (sampled twice a second with psutil, or resource.getrusage without it — the sampling field says which); GET /api/jobs/<id>/result returns a finished payload unchanged; POST /api/jobs/<id>/cancel kills the worker, and the original request answers {"ok": false, "error": "cancelled"}; POST /api/jobs/clear drops finished jobs. The registry keeps the last 50 jobs (at most 10 lints) and 64 MB of payloads, evicting payloads first. Windows keep only a job id and source hash, so a result survives closing its window; an evicted one offers to run again.
Editor intelligence. Lint, completion and signatures are static — nothing is imported or run — and answered in the server process: POST /api/lint (ruff, ~6 ms), POST /api/complete (jedi, ~15 ms), POST /api/signature (~2 ms). Diagnostics are red (errors), amber (likely mistakes) or blue (style), with ruff’s fixes offered as actions, and a failed compile’s traceback line is underlined until the text changes. Completions resolve against the installed cadjoint. Without the editor extra the endpoints return an install hint and the editor stays quiet.
Scenes API. GET /api/scenes, POST /api/scenes/load and POST /api/scenes/save refuse path separators, traversal and hidden files before touching the filesystem. POST /api/export returns the file with Content-Disposition and the job id in X-Cadjoint-Job.

title: Playground
text:
Developing the UI
The app is a Solid + TypeScript project in frontend/, built into cadjoint/viewer/static and committed, so installing cadjoint needs no Node toolchain.
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev        # Vite on :5173, proxying the API to the Python server
npm run build      # refresh cadjoint/viewer/static (commit the result)
npm test           # unit tests (vitest)
npm run e2e        # Playwright, drives the real server end to end
Run uv run cadjoint-viewer alongside npm run dev so the dev server has an API to proxy to. Help › Design language opens the interface’s design rules and the feature index the menus are generated from.

title: Playground
text:
Troubleshooting
WebGPU is unavailable. Use a WebGPU-capable browser with hardware acceleration enabled. The editor still compiles, and Help › Developer › Show generated WGSL still shows the shader.
The command is not found. Run python -m cadjoint.viewer.playground --open, or reinstall so the cadjoint-viewer console script is created.
It stops at startup with No module named 'pydantic'. The viewer extra is missing: pip install "cadjoint[viewer,editor]", or uv sync --extra viewer --extra editor in a checkout.

title: SDF
text:
SDF()
Abstract base class for Signed Distance Functions.
An SDF represents geometry implicitly as a function f(p) -> distance, where: - f(p) < 0: point p is inside the shape - f(p) = 0: point p is on the surface - f(p) > 0: point p is outside the shape










Name
Type
Description




params
dict[str, Parameter]
Dictionary of Parameter objects for this SDF operation



SDF classes are thin wrappers around pure functions: - Provide fluent API: .translate().rotate() chaining - Enable operators: sphere | box, sphere & box - Store parameters for later compilation - Actual computation happens in pure functions
Each SDF instance should store its parameters in self.params dictionary: self.params = { ‘radius’: Scalar(value=1.0, free=True, name=‘radius’), ‘offset’: Vector(value=[0, 0, 0], free=False), }
Subclasses must implement: - @staticmethod def sdf(…): Pure function for computation (CONVENTION) - call(p): Evaluate SDF (delegates to sdf())



@staticmethod def sdf(p: Array, param1: float, param2: float) -> Array: # Pure computation here
def call(self, p: Array) -> Array: return ClassName.sdf(p, self.params[‘param1’].value, self.params[‘param2’].value)



@staticmethod def sdf(child_sdf: Callable, p: Array, param: float) -> Array: # Transform computation here
def call(self, p: Array) -> Array: return ClassName.sdf(self.child_sdf, p, self.params[‘param’].value)

Description

Return material properties at point p.

Return this node’s smooth patch fields in its own frame, if known.

required

SDF.patch_fields()
Return this node’s smooth patch fields in its own frame, if known.
A patch field decomposition expresses the node’s surface as pieces of the zero sets of smooth scalar fields f_i — the node’s SDF is internally a min/max composition over them (Box: six face half-space distances; Cylinder: side plus two caps). A surface point p belongs to patch argmin_i |f_i(p)|, and the node’s exact feature edges are exactly where that ownership switches.
Transforms forward the protocol by mapping the query point into the child frame exactly as their sdf does. Nodes without an exact decomposition return None (the default), which consumers treat gracefully as “one opaque patch”.

title: backends.compile_scene_to_wgsl
text:
backends.compile_scene_to_wgsl(
    geometry,
    example_point=None,
    *,
    uniforms=False,
    culling=True,
    scope='free',
)
Compile an SDF and its material evaluation to one WGSL module.
The returned source has three stable point-query functions:

sdf(p) -> f32
material_base(p) -> vec4<f32> containing RGB and roughness
material_optics(p) -> vec4<f32> containing metallic, opacity, IOR, and reflectivity

All functions are built from the same functionalized geometry snapshot, so CSG material selection and transformed material coordinates match the distance field. Generated helper functions are namespaced per entry point, making the returned source safe to embed as one WGSL module.
Design parameters are inlined as float literals by default, which is what the frontend consumes today: the whole module changes when any value does. Pass uniforms=True for the form that reads them out of a uniform buffer instead — see :func:compile_scene_with_uniforms, whose :class:ShaderProgram this then returns in place of the source string.

Type

Default

Root CADJOINT SDF node with optional per-primitive materials.
required

Example input for shape inference. Defaults to zeros.
None

bool
Emit parameters as a uniform buffer rather than as literals, returning a :class:ShaderProgram instead of a string.
False


culling
bool
Skip a boolean’s far-away operands with a real branch (see :mod:cadjoint.backends.wgsl._culling). The field is identical either way; off is the flat form the culled one is tested against.
True


scope
str
Which parameters the uniform buffer holds when uniforms is set — "free" or "all". Ignored otherwise. See :func:compile_scene_with_uniforms for why the default is "free" and why "all" must not be shipped.
'free'

backends.wgsl.ShaderParameter(name, offset, components, value, free, depends=())
One design parameter’s place in the generated uniform buffer.










Name
Type
Description

str
The parameter’s name — a free parameter’s declared name, or a fixed parameter’s node.attribute path. The same names :func:cadjoint.extract_parameters returns.

int
Byte offset into the uniform buffer. Always a multiple of :data:PARAMETER_SLOT_BYTES.

int
How many floats the parameter occupies (1-4); the rest of its 16-byte slot is padding.


value
tuple[float, …]
The parameter’s current value, as a list of floats.

bool
Whether it is a free (named, optimizable) parameter.

tuple[str, …]
For a slot derived from the parameters (a culling box), the names of the slots it was computed from; empty otherwise.









Name
Description




as_dict
This entry as a plain JSON-serializable dict.





backends.wgsl.ShaderParameter.as_dict()
This entry as a plain JSON-serializable dict.
A value component that is not finite travels as null. JSON has no NaN — Python’s encoder writes a bare NaN that no strict parser, the browser’s JSON.parse included, will read — and these are not rare: a Material that leaves its physical properties unset (density, conductivity, Young’s modulus …) carries a NaN in every one of them, so almost every scene has some.
The null is not a substitution. Whoever packs the buffer turns it back into a NaN, because a NaN is what the literal form inlines into the same slot; the two forms must render the same image, and that includes agreeing about the values nobody supplied.

title: backends.wgsl.compile_scene_with_uniforms
text:
backends.wgsl.compile_scene_with_uniforms(
    geometry,
    example_point=None,
    *,
    group=DEFAULT_PARAMETER_GROUP,
    binding=DEFAULT_PARAMETER_BINDING,
    culling=True,
    scope='free',
)
Compile a scene to WGSL whose parameters live in a uniform buffer.
:func:compile_scene_to_wgsl folds every design parameter into the shader as a float literal, so moving one slider by 0.05 rewrites three lines of a 139 kB module and forces the browser to recompile all of it. Here the same parameters are function arguments read out of a uniform block instead: the source is byte-identical for every value of every parameter, and an edit is a buffer write and a redraw.
The buffer is an array of vec4<f32> — one 16-byte slot per parameter, which is the only element type a WGSL uniform array carries without per-field alignment rules — declared as::
struct SdfParameters { values: array<vec4<f32>, N> };
@group(G) @binding(B) var<storage, read> sdf_parameters: SdfParameters;
Parameters a pattern consumes structurally (a count) keep their slot but are never read: the instance count decides how much shader gets emitted, so it cannot be edited without recompiling.
Only the free parameters get a slot, and that is the whole design. A value the shader reads from a buffer is a value the GPU’s compiler cannot fold, and folding is not a minor optimisation here — it is what makes the generated field affordable at all. Measured on this machine’s Metal adapter, scenes/end_cap.py at 1200x800:
====================================== ========== =========== form preview path sample ====================================== ========== =========== every parameter in the buffer (330) 106.2 ms 185.7 ms every parameter a literal 4.0 ms 41.5 ms only the 11 free parameters buffered 3.3 ms 36.1 ms ====================================== ========== ===========
All three draw the same image to the last pixel. The cost is not the loads — hoisting all 4 560 of them to 671 changed nothing — and it is not the shape of the emitted code: substituting the literals back into the all-uniform module, structure untouched, recovers the full speed. It is that scenes/end_cap.py is 1.7 MB of WGSL because it is mostly constant-foldable: 21 pattern instances, each unrolled with its own transform algebra, which collapses to a handful of instructions per instance when the transform is known and runs in full when it is not.
The free parameters are the ones a handle drags and an optimizer moves, they are two orders of magnitude fewer (11 against 319 here), and the subtrees they unfold are the ones being edited anyway. A fixed parameter — a node attribute typed into the inspector — still costs a recompile. That is the trade, and it is the right way round.

title: cache.prune_compilation_cache
text:
cache.prune_compilation_cache(
    directory=None,
    max_bytes=_MAX_BYTES,
    *,
    force=False,
)
Delete the oldest cache entries until the directory fits max_bytes.
Runs at most once per :data:_PRUNE_INTERVAL_SECONDS unless force: the check is one stat of a stamp file, cheap enough for every worker process to make. Age is the later of an entry’s access and modification time, so on a filesystem that records reads it is least-recently-used, and least-recently-written otherwise. It also removes the -atime files JAX’s own eviction left beside every entry; nothing reads them once that eviction is off.

constraints.project_to_manifold(free_params, metadata, *, steps=1)
Project free_params onto the constraint manifold via Newton correction(s).
Applies steps Newton steps: Δ = Jᵀ(JJᵀ)⁻¹ c(p), p ← p − Δ. One step is exact for linear constraints and first-order accurate for nonlinear ones (e.g. sphere). Increase steps for tighter satisfaction.

title: construction.Face
text:
construction.Face(
    kind,
    key,
    origin,
    normal,
    x_axis,
    boundary,
    *,
    owner=None,
    reference=None,
)
One analytic planar face of a construction feature.
A face is a reference, not stored geometry: its origin and boundary are recomputed from the feature’s parameters every time the feature is built, so a sketch placed on it follows the parent and gradients flow through it.











Name
Type
Description
Default




kind
str
cap (an extrusion or loft end), side (a swept polygon edge), or planar (a primitive’s flat face).
required


key
str
Identity of the face within its owner — cap+, side3, +x. Stable across rebuilds, so the viewer can address it.
required


origin

A point on the face, in world space.
required


normal

Outward face normal in world space; normalized on construction.
required


x_axis

The face’s in-plane “horizontal”; orthogonalized against the normal so the frame is orthonormal whatever the caller passes.
required


boundary

The face’s boundary loop in world space, shape (M, 3).
required


owner

The feature or primitive that declared the face.
None


reference
tuple[str, tuple] | None
(method, args) naming the accessor that returns this face — ("cap", ("+",)) — which is what the viewer writes back into the user’s source.
None









Name
Description




y_axis
The in-plane axis completing a right-handed frame with the normal.









Name
Description




center
The centroid of the face’s boundary loop, in world space.


contains
Whether a world point lies on this face, within tol.


describe
Serialize the face for the viewer.


diagonal
Diagonal of the face’s bounding box — the scale a tolerance is read against.


frame
Return the orthonormal (x, y, normal) frame of the face.


hole
A cylindrical tool sunk into this face — subtract it to cut a hole.


plane
This face as a sketch plane, optionally pushed along its normal.


pocket
A prismatic tool sunk into this face — subtract it to cut a pocket.


point
A world point at face-local coordinates at, measured from the origin.


polygon
The boundary loop in face coordinates, shape (M, 2).


to_local
Project world points (..., 3) onto the face’s (..., 2) axes.


tolerance
Default hit tolerance for :meth:contains, scaled to the face.





construction.Face.center()
The centroid of the face’s boundary loop, in world space.
The natural anchor for a feature placed “on the middle of this face” — a boss, a bore, a bolt circle’s axis — and, being an average of the boundary, an expression in the parent’s parameters like everything else on the face.





Name
Type
Description





Array
The centroid, shape (3,).







construction.Face.contains(point, tol=None)
Whether a world point lies on this face, within tol.
Two tests, both inclusive of the tolerance: the point must sit within tol of the face’s plane, and its in-plane projection must lie inside the boundary polygon (again allowing tol of slack, so a hit exactly on a shared edge belongs to both faces rather than neither).

construction.Face.hole(
    radius,
    depth,
    at=(0.0, 0.0),
    *,
    through=0.0,
    material=None,
)
A cylindrical tool sunk into this face — subtract it to cut a hole.
Returns the tool rather than a modified solid, because in an implicit modeller the cut is the boolean: keeping them separate is what lets one tool be patterned, mirrored, or subtracted from several bodies at once, and what keeps the hole visible in the feature tree.
The tool is a true :class:~cadjoint.sdf.primitives.cylinder.Cylinder aligned with the face normal, not a polygonal approximation, so the bore stays round at every render scale and its radius stays a live design parameter.











Name
Type
Description
Default




radius

Bore radius; may be a Scalar parameter.
required


depth

How far the tool reaches below the face, along -normal. May be a Scalar.
required


at

Where the axis meets the face, in face-local (x, y).
(0.0, 0.0)


through
float
Extra length added above the face. Zero leaves the tool exactly flush, which is what a blind hole wants; a small positive value keeps a through-hole’s mouth off the surface it is cutting, where a perfectly coincident pair of surfaces would otherwise leave the mesher to break the tie.
0.0


material

Optional render material for the tool.
None









Name
Type
Description






The tool as an SDF, placed in world space.






bore = flange.cap("+").hole(bore_radius, depth=0.4, through=0.02)
housing = Difference(flange, bore)

)
A cylindrical tool sunk into this face — subtract it to cut a hole.
Returns the tool rather than a modified solid, because in an implicit modeller the cut is the boolean: keeping them separate is what lets one tool be patterned, mirrored, or subtracted from several bodies at once, and what keeps the hole visible in the feature tree.

A work plane the sketch entities live on.

construction.SketchPlane.tangent(
    solid,
    near,
    x_axis=None,
    *,
    max_step=1.0,
    steps=8,
    normal_step=0.001,
)
The tangent plane of an SDF at the surface point nearest near.
This is the reference for everything with no analytic face: blends, fillets, the curved wall of a revolve. near is Newton-projected onto the zero set with :func:cadjoint.fem.motion.project_points, and the plane’s normal is read off the field by a central difference across the surface — both differentiable, so the plane tracks the scene’s parameters rather than a snapshot of them. The difference is used in place of jax.grad because the surface is exactly where a CSG field changes branch; see :func:_surface_normal.











Name
Type
Description
Default




solid

Any callable scalar field on (3,) points — an SDF instance is one.
required


near

A world point at or near the surface; a raymarch hit is the intended source.
required


x_axis

Override the in-plane horizontal; defaults to the world axis most nearly inside the tangent plane.
None


max_step
float
Cap on how far the projection may move near.
1.0


steps
int
Newton iterations.
8


normal_step
float
Half-width of the central difference that reads the normal. Raise it on a field that is noisy at the surface, lower it where two faces meet within a thousandth.
0.001









Name
Type
Description






The tangent plane at the projected point.

SDF solid sharing parameter references with the construction tree. title: enums.Precision
text:
enums.Precision()
The floating-point width a descent runs in.
A property of the run, not of the objective: a solver may scope double precision around its own forward pass (:func:cadjoint.flow.precision.double_precision does), but :func:jax.grad runs the transposed pass after that scope has closed, so the flag has to be held for the whole loop or the backward pass meets float64 intermediates it cannot materialise. Declaring it on the optimization rather than at a scene’s module scope is what keeps the scene float32 for the WGSL shader, which has no f64.





Name
Description




DOUBLE
jax_enable_x64 for the duration of the run, restored after.


SINGLE
Whatever the process is already in (the default).

fem.HexMesh.moved(field, *, smooth_passes=0, design=None)
Node positions under the design: snapped vertices re-projected, the lattice frozen.
With a table and the design’s parameters, each snapped vertex is solved onto the census surfaces it was classified on — a crease vertex onto both faces at once — which is the derivative a single field’s Newton gets wrong there. Without, the single field’s.

title: fem.gmsh.assign_ownership
text:
fem.gmsh.assign_ownership(fields, topology, *, bar)
Tag every node with the patches that own it, by residual alone.
Per Gmsh surface entity, |f_p| is evaluated on its nodes for every patch; the patches whose worst node clears bar are the candidates, and the one with the smallest typical residual owns the surface. The maximum, not the median, is what separates a mesh from a spoiled one: an entity straddling a blend’s edge has most of its nodes hugging the neighbouring plane and a few peeling away, and judged by the median it would pass as that plane — the projection would then drag the peeling nodes onto the plane’s unbounded extension. Curve and point nodes inherit their bounding surfaces’ patches and keep those that vanish at the node itself, up to the entity’s codimension.

title: fem.recompute_tet_points
text:
fem.recompute_tet_points(sdf, mesh, *, smooth_passes=0)
Recompute tet-mesh vertex positions differentiably with frozen topology.
The leading num_surface boundary vertices are Newton re-projected from their frozen nominal positions onto the (possibly traced) SDF’s zero set — the same clamped projection the hex mesher uses, so the output is a differentiable function of the SDF’s parameters. Interior Steiner vertices stay frozen by default; smooth_passes > 0 runs that many differentiable Jacobi–Laplacian passes propagating the boundary displacement inward (boundary values pinned), which keeps interior elements better shaped under larger design motions. On a TET10 mesh the midside nodes are recomputed as midpoints of the traced corner positions, so gradients flow through them too.

title: flow.EnergyConfig
text:
flow.EnergyConfig(
    shape,
    fluid_diffusivity,
    conductivity_ratio=200.0,
    inlet_temperature=0.0,
    wall_temperature=None,
    scheme='exponential',
    tol=1e-10,
    max_steps=4000,
    restart=60,
)
Static settings for one conjugate energy solve.










Name
Type
Description




shape
tuple[int, int, int]
(NX, NY, NZ) lattice, duct axis along +Y, matching the momentum solve’s grid exactly.


fluid_diffusivity
float
The air’s thermal diffusivity in lattice units, nu / Pr. Numerically also its conductivity, because (rho cp)_f is the unit of this system.


conductivity_ratio
float
k_solid / k_fluid. Aluminium in air is about 8000; a ratio that large is physically right and numerically punishing (see the module docstring on conditioning), so a study that only needs “much better than air” is better served by a few hundred.


inlet_temperature
float
Temperature carried in at the inlet plane.


wall_temperature
float | None
Temperature of the duct’s lateral walls, or None (the default) for adiabatic walls — the right choice for a duct that is not itself a heat exchanger.


scheme
str
"exponential" or "upwind"; see the module docstring.


tol
float
Relative residual the linear solve stops at.


max_steps
int
Iteration cap for the linear solve.


restart
int
Krylov subspace size before GMRES restarts, and the one setting here that can silently return a wrong answer. Restarted GMRES stagnates when the subspace is too small for the operator’s spectrum, and the conductivity ratio is what sets that spectrum: on a 14x26x14 duct, restart = 30 converges to 2.9e-12 at a ratio of 50 and stalls at a relative residual of 0.23 at a ratio of 200 – reporting a peak temperature of 0.014 where the answer is 0.602, with no error and no warning. 60 converges at both. It costs restart stored fields, which is the reason not to simply set it very high on a large lattice. :func:energy_imbalance is the check that catches a stall, and :attr:~cadjoint.flow.study.FlowStudyResult.warnings runs it.

Type
Description





ValueError
On a non-positive diffusivity or conductivity ratio, or an unknown scheme.

Declared in a scene exactly like :class:~cadjoint.fem.study.ThermalStudy – constructing one inside :func:~cadjoint.studies.capture_studies registers it – but it meshes nothing. The lattice is fixed and the design enters as a field on it, which is why the whole solve stays one differentiable JAX expression.

title: flow.heat_transfer_proxy
text:
flow.heat_transfer_proxy(chi, u, cell_volume=1.0)
int chi |u| – air in motion where the metal is.
A stand-in for the surface heat-transfer coefficient, and a cheap one: it needs no surface extraction, only the two fields already in hand. Deep inside the solid it contributes nothing (the drag has killed u there) and far outside it contributes nothing (chi is zero), so what it actually measures is flow speed in the interface band – which is where convective cooling happens.
Its known weakness is that it is a volume integral over a band whose thickness is set by epsilon, so comparing two designs at different grid resolutions needs the same epsilon in world units. The surface-weighted variant int |grad chi| |u| removes that dependence at the cost of a finite-difference gradient of chi; see research/flow-solver.md.

title: functionalize
text:
functionalize
Compile parameterized SDF trees to pure JAX functions.
The SDF tree is cadjoint’s intermediate representation: primitives, booleans, transforms and patterns, each with named parameter slots. This module lowers it to JAX, and how it does that decides how big the compiled program is.
Traced naively, the tree flattens: a pattern of eight ribs emits eight copies of the rib, a subtree used by two booleans is emitted twice, and every parameter value is folded in as a literal — so a slider edit produces a program that is structurally identical to the one before it and yet compiles from scratch. Three things keep that from happening here.

Sharing. A node is built once per object, not once per occurrence, so a tool cut from several bodies is one function.
Outlining. A node that is evaluated more than once — a pattern’s child, a shared subtree — is wrapped in :func:jax.jit, which StableHLO keeps as a func.func and a func.call per instance. The WGSL backend already emits one shader function per func.func, so the same move shrinks the shader.
Parameters as arguments. :func:functionalize_parametric hands the parameter dicts to the jitted function rather than closing over them, so the lowered HLO is byte-identical across value edits and the persistent compilation cache hits.

Everything is opt-out through :func:cadjoint.sdf._lowering.scalar_lowering, which the shader backend holds while it traces: WGSL has no type wider than a mat4, so the array-shaped forms inside the primitives cannot be lowered there and the flat emission is still the right one.

Description

functionalize_parametric
Compile an SDF to a function whose parameters are arguments.

Compile a geometry SDF tree to pure (sdf, material_fn) closures.

Compile a scene so its parameters are arguments, not literals.

title: materials.fr4
text:
materials.fr4()
FR-4 woven-glass/epoxy laminate — the standard PCB substrate.
FR-4 is orthotropic and the solver is isotropic, so this entry takes the through-thickness thermal conductivity (0.29 W/(mK)) — the number that matters for getting heat out of a board — together with the in-plane elastic constants and in-plane CTE, which is what board-level warpage and stiffness depend on. In-plane conductivity is roughly 0.8–1.0 W/(mK) and the out-of-plane CTE above Tg is several times the in-plane value; model those explicitly if they drive your result. yield_strength holds the ultimate tensile strength: FR-4 is brittle and has no yield plateau, so a “safety factor” against it is a factor against fracture.
Sources: NEMA LI-1 / IPC-4101 FR-4 specifications; Isola 370HR and Rogers laminate datasheets; Sarvar, Poole & Witting, J. Electron. Mater. 19 (1990) on PCB thermal conductivity.

title: materials.silicon
text:
materials.silicon()
Single-crystal silicon, intrinsic, at 300 K — dies and MEMS.
Silicon is elastically anisotropic; this entry uses the ⟨100⟩ direction (E = 130 GPa, ν = 0.28), which is the wafer-normal direction for standard (100) wafers. ⟨110⟩ and ⟨111⟩ reach 169 GPa and 188 GPa respectively. yield_strength holds a practical fracture strength: silicon is brittle with no yield point, and measured fracture strength is dominated by surface and edge damage, ranging from ~100 MPa for a sawn edge to several GPa for a pristine etched surface — 165 MPa is a conservative die-level figure.
Sources: Hopcroft, Nix & Kenny, “What is the Young’s Modulus of Silicon?”, J. Microelectromech. Syst. 19(2):229–238, 2010; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density, conductivity, specific heat, CTE).

A filled-silicone thermal interface pad (gap filler).
Representative of a 3 W/(mK) gap pad such as Henkel Bergquist Gap Pad 3000S30. title: meshing.manifold_cell_incidence
text:
meshing.manifold_cell_incidence(edges, grid, inside)
Group crossing edges by cell and by inside-corner component.
Uniform dual contouring places one vertex per active cell, which cannot represent two surface sheets crossing the same cell: their quads share the vertex and mesh edges end up bordered by four triangles. Following Manifold Dual Contouring, this variant splits every active cell into the connected components of its inside corners under the cell’s edge adjacency (corners connected along the twelve cell edges) and emits one incidence row per component. Each crossing edge joins the component of its inside endpoint, so a cell crossed by two sheets contributes two rows — two QEF vertices — and the quads of the two sheets stay disjoint. Cells crossed by a single sheet produce exactly the rows (and slot order) of :func:cell_edge_incidence.

title: meshing.qef_vertices
text:
meshing.qef_vertices(hermite, incidence, grid, *, regularization=0.001)
Place one vertex per active cell from its Hermite tangent planes.
Minimizes Σ (nᵢ · (v - pᵢ))² plus a Tikhonov pull toward the cell’s Hermite mass point, scaled so regularization is relative to the normal count. Planar cells (rank-1 systems) land on the face near the mass point, crease cells slide onto the crease line, and corner cells reproduce the corner; the bias a corner inherits from the regularization is of order regularization × cell size.
Fully JAX-traceable: call under jax.grad/jax.jit with a hermite built from traced parameters to differentiate vertex positions. Vertices are clamped to their cell as a final safety net; the clamp binds only on degenerate cells.

title: meshing.save_step
text:
meshing.save_step(mesh, path)
Write a minimal faceted STEP AP214 boundary representation.
Builds one planar ADVANCED_FACE per merged polygon (via :func:merge_planar_faces) and per leftover triangle, over shared VERTEX_POINT and EDGE_CURVE/LINE topology, gathered into a CLOSED_SHELL inside a MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP with the minimal AP214 product and unit boilerplate. Every referenced entity id is defined and the output is deterministic for a given mesh.
Degenerate loop edges (endpoints closer than the file’s declared distance accuracy, which sharp feature placement can produce) are welded away first — OCCT rejects zero-length LINE geometry and would split the shell. Output is validated against the OCCT kernel in tests/meshing/test_step_kernel.py: files read back as a single valid closed MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP with matching face counts and volume. Units are metres (one mesh unit = 1 m); readers defaulting to millimetres scale coordinates by 1000 on import.

title: meshing.sharp_qef_vertices
text:
meshing.sharp_qef_vertices
meshing.sharp_qef_vertices(hermite, incidence, grid, *, rcond=0.05)
Place vertices with a rank-revealing QEF that lands exactly on features.
The truncated pseudo-inverse keeps only the constraint directions the cell’s Hermite planes actually determine: planar cells project the mass point onto their face, crease cells land on the crease line, and corner cells reproduce the corner — with none of the mass-point bias the Tikhonov solve trades for smooth gradients. On a uniform grid that bias differs per cell (it depends on how the grid slices the surface), which is exactly the wiggle visible along feature curves.
Concrete forward placement only: singular-value truncation has no usable derivative, so optimization losses should keep differentiating :func:qef_vertices. The two solutions differ by the regularization bias, of order regularization × cell size. Vertices always stay in their cell: candidate solutions at every truncation rank are clamped to the cell and the one with the smallest QEF error wins, so a marginal singular direction that flings the full-rank minimizer outside cannot park the vertex off the surface.

    mesh,

    preserve_features=True,

Every node of a Gmsh mesh, with the patches that own it — the seam’s record.
Produced by the public Gmsh route (:func:cadjoint.fem.gmsh.assign_ownership, a residual test against the scene’s public patch fields and nothing else) and consumed by the private node_map, which re-solves each node against its owners under a design change. title: plugins.registry
text:
plugins.registry
Which component plays which cadjoint kind, and where it runs.
This is the part that is genuinely cadjoint’s: a name -> spec table, a kind -> name default, and three places a spec can come from, later ones winning:

Built-ins — the Tesseract packages in this repository (:data:BUILTIN_PACKAGES), as local specs. Nothing shipped here fills the private tier’s five in-process kinds; the diff-brep distribution registers those through the entry-point group below, and :mod:cadjoint.tier says so in one sentence when it is absent.
Entry points — the cadjoint.plugins group. A distribution registers a component by exposing a :class:~cadjoint.plugins.PluginSpec, a mapping in the plugins.toml table form, or a callable returning either.
The config file — plugins.toml, found at $CADJOINT_PLUGINS (a file, or a directory holding one) or else $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cadjoint/plugins.toml (default ~/.config/cadjoint/plugins.toml). A table whose name matches an existing plugin replaces its spec — that is how the thermal solver moves from this process to a cluster URL without a line of code changing.

The file has two tables::
[defaults]                       # which plugin fills each slot
elastic_solver = "elastic_calculix"

[plugins.thermal_jaxfem]         # where a plugin runs
kind = "thermal_solver"
transport = "remote"
url = "http://thermal.cadjoint.svc.cluster.local:8000"
schema_hash = "sha256:2a1f..."
Seeing the public tier. sdf.Difference(*sdfs, smoothness=0.1)
Difference of SDFs (subtract all subsequent from first).
Uses smooth maximum for differentiable blending.

Type

Tuple of SDFs; first is the base, rest are subtracted
()


smoothness
float
Blend half-width in model units, not a fillet radius. 0 is a sharp boolean; the default of 0.1 blends, so a plain Difference(a, b) is a blended one and a caller who wants the sharp operation has to ask for smoothness=0. The value does not scale with the part: 0.1 is a tenth of a unit whatever the unit stands for, enough on a large part to erase a thin internal feature. See :mod:cadjoint.sdf.boolean.smooth for what the blend costs — it moves the field by up to smoothness per operation, and by the full amount wherever the operands agree.

sdf.Difference.material_at(p)
The body’s material, tinted by each tool near the surface that tool cut.
Folds over every tool, the way :meth:Union.material_at folds over every operand, so a part cut by more than one tool takes its material from every cut, not just the first.



sdf.Difference.patch_fields()
Body patches then tool patches, operand-major, for a sharp cut only.
max(body, -tool_1, -tool_2, ...), so the result’s surface is the body’s surface where no tool reaches plus each tool’s surface where it cut into the body — pieces of the operands’ surfaces and nothing else. The fields are theirs concatenated in operand order, with every tool negated, exactly as the composition negates it: a tool’s own field reads positive outside the tool, which is inside the cavity it left, so leaving it alone would hand the consumer a patch whose normal points into the material. Negating flips it to positive outside the result, and leaves the zero set — hence argmin |f_i| ownership — untouched.
See :func:~cadjoint.sdf.boolean.base._operand_patch_fields for the order’s guarantees and why a smoothness > 0 difference declines.
